title: Evidence manifest: What Should a Temporal Contact Generator Actually Model?
how_to_read: One object per evidence block of docs/index.html. 'evidence' lists the verified claims with their report, result files, metric and numbers (value, source file, locator); 'figures' lists every chart of the block with the module that builds it and the result files it reads. Paths without a leading 'docs/' or 'scripts/' are relative to the result root.
result_root: /result/uhnam/dexcore (the server's result tree; small source tables are snapshotted under docs/data/sources/)

page_headings: With predicted contact, the hand error is higher on every split
source_labels: BimArt → TACO port (generation 3) · BimArt upstream analysis

figures.title: Hand error with the ground-truth contact map versus the predicted one

source_files.locator: rows split = test_1, test_2, test_3, test_4; columns motion_kp_err_mm_gt_contact (GT contact) and motion_kp_err_mm_pred_contact (predicted contact); column sampled = windows scored
windows.<window>.'GT contact'.total_mm and windows.<window>.'stage-1 contact'.total_mm, all windows in file order; samples_per_arm

figures.note: Position error of the generated hand keypoints in mm (lower is better) when the motion stage is conditioned on the ground-truth contact map versus on the contact stage's own prediction, with the same motion model and sampling procedure in both arms. TACO: mean distance over 200 keypoints and 64 frames, 128 sampled windows per split, one sample each; ARCTIC: per-hand RMSE on 8 windows from 2 laptop sequences, 3 samples per arm; the metrics differ, so the panels are not comparable in level, and there are no error bars because neither table gives an interval. The ground-truth arm is an oracle: its contact map is computed from the recorded hands. TACO: this project's port of BimArt, one training run; test_1 was the validation split used to select the checkpoints, so test_2 to test_4 are the unbiased splits. ARCTIC: the released checkpoints, with upstream's cost guidance, which also reads the arm's contact map; the two TACO columns are sampled without cost guidance.

evidence.claim: In this project's port of the two-stage BimArt generator to TACO (generation 3, the current one), conditioning the motion stage on the contact stage's own prediction instead of the ground-truth contact map raises the mean hand-keypoint error on every official test split (37.1 -> 58.6, 48.8 -> 86.5, 63.4 -> 104.9, 50.9 -> 79.8 mm), which supports reading contact prediction as a major source of downstream hand error.
evidence.metric: Mean Euclidean distance (mm, lower is better) between generated and recorded hand keypoints, over 200 keypoints (100 MANO surface points per hand), the 64 frames of a window and 128 windows sampled per test split (seed 0, one sample per window, 50-step sampling, EMA weights, classifier-free guidance 0.5). Compared: the same motion model and the same noise seed, conditioned on the ground-truth (recorded) contact map versus on the contact stage's prediction. No interval is stored for these values.

TACO | checkpoints and inference setting.value: contact model_best.pth (contact_epoch 62), motion model_best.pth+ema (motion_epoch 17), cfg_strength 0.5, ema true, seed 0, sample_windows 128

TACO | same table as quoted in the repor.locator: columns gt_scene and pred_scene, rows test_1..test_4

caveats: This is the project's own port of BimArt to TACO (generation 3 of three), not a number published by BimArt's authors.
One training run, one sampling seed, one sample per window, 128 sampled windows per split; no confidence interval exists for the gap between the two columns.
The ground-truth-contact arm is an oracle condition: the map is computed from the recorded hands.
Even with the ground-truth map the motion stage is 37-63 mm off on the test splits, so contact prediction is a major source of error, not the only one.
The validation split was test_1 in every run, so model_best was selected on test_1; test_2, test_3 and test_4 are the unbiased splits (scene_reverification.md section 3; VERDICT_scene.json caveats).
Do not subtract the two columns to get a 'share due to contact': the attribution script's docstring states that distances do not add linearly.
The report prose gives the best epochs as contact 61 / motion 16; evaluation/meta.json stores 62 / 17 (checkpoint epoch + 1). Same checkpoints.

evidence.claim: Starting both samplings from the same initial noise (seed 0), the displacement between the hand generated with the predicted contact map and the hand generated with the ground-truth map (40.5 / 65.6 / 74.8 / 61.2 mm) is larger than the motion stage's own error under the ground-truth map (38.0 / 56.4 / 71.9 / 52.4 mm) on all four TACO test splits (64 sampled windows per split, generation 3, no interval, pooled over the two hands); the source table's ratio contact / (contact + motion) is 0.51-0.54, a ratio of two mean magnitudes and not a fraction of the total error.
evidence.metric: Same-seed stage attribution on 64 sampled windows per test split (seed 0), generation 3. The motion model is sampled twice from the same noise, on the recorded contact map (x_gt) and on the predicted one (x_pred). motion_mm = mean |x_gt - recorded|; contact_mm = mean |x_pred - x_gt|; total_mm = mean |x_pred - recorded|; all over 200 hand keypoints and 64 frames, in mm, lower is better. cos = mean cosine between the two displacement vectors. share_contact = contact_mm / (motion_mm + contact_mm), a ratio of two mean magnitudes. No interval stored.

TACO | report PROSE for the same quantit.value: "The contact stage still accounts for 51-54% of the total error" / "the contact stage is half of BimArt's error on TACO"

caveats: PROSE vs TABLE: the report says '51-54% of the total error'; the table column is contact_mm / (motion_mm + contact_mm). The two displacement vectors are near-orthogonal (cos 0.05-0.10), so motion_mm + contact_mm exceeds total_mm (test_1: 37.98 + 40.55 against 59.78). It is a ratio of two stage magnitudes, not a fraction of the measured total error and not a causal share.

64 sampled windows per split, one seed, no interval. A different window sample than the 128-window evaluation and the all-window probe, so its totals (59.8 / 95.9 / 113.1 / 85.7 mm) differ from theirs; never mix the three in one comparison.
TACO only. No such ratio exists for ARCTIC or OakInk2.
Generation 3 only for the current state; the generation-1 row is the defective-label model and is legitimate only as the 'before' value.
evidence.claim_as_extracted: With the sampling noise held fixed, the displacement of the generated hand caused by replacing the ground-truth contact map with the predicted one (40.5-74.8 mm) is at least as large as the motion stage's own error under the ground-truth map (38.0-71.9 mm) on all four TACO test splits; the source table's ratio contact / (contact + motion) is 0.51-0.54.
evidence.correction_reason: Numbers confirmed in attribution/stage_attribution.csv. Two wording problems: (1) 'sampling noise held fixed' is not what the code does: only the starting noise x_T is seeded; sched.step is called without a generator, so the per-step DDPM noise differs between the two arms (eval_bimart_taco.py lines 94-114); (2) 'caused by' is on the avoid list and the displacement includes that unshared noise. The ratio wording is fine as long as its definition stays next to it.

evidence.claim: Over every window of the four TACO test splits and pooled over the two hands, the same decomposition gives a contact-stage component (41.7 / 59.4 / 70.0 / 55.0 mm) larger than the motion-stage component (37.9 / 49.9 / 62.1 / 51.3 mm), whereas on the 640-window training subsample it is smaller (12.0 against 13.9 mm). Per hand the picture differs: the contact-stage component exceeds the motion-stage one for the left (target-holding) hand on all four test splits (49.0 / 70.7 / 76.8 / 62.6 against 36.6 / 43.8 / 50.9 / 42.3 mm) and is smaller for the right (tool-holding) hand (34.3 / 48.0 / 63.2 / 47.3 against 39.3 / 56.0 / 73.3 / 60.3 mm). The contact stage's test_1 / train ratio (3.46) is higher than the motion stage's (2.72), which is consistent with the contact stage generalising worse; no interval exists for these levels or ratios.
evidence.metric: Per-window probe of generation 3 (column 'scene'), same construction as the attribution: motion_mm = mean |x_gt - recorded| (hand error with the ground-truth contact map), contact_mm = mean |x_pred - x_gt|, total_mm = mean |x_pred - recorded| (hand error with the predicted map); mm, lower is better; mean over window-hands (every test window x 2 hands; train = a 640-window subsample). Ratios test_1 / train are of these split means.
caveats: The train row is a 640-window subsample (1280 window-hands), the test rows are every window.
test_1 is the validation split used for checkpoint selection in every run; the ratio is against test_1 only.
The split means carry no interval in this table (the lo / hi columns are for the generation-3 minus generation-1 delta, not for these levels).
One training run and one sampling seed.
'Generalising worse' is the report's reading of a ratio of two split means; the report also states that the relative gap did not shrink after the label fix (2.84 -> 3.46).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: Over every window of the four TACO test splits, the same decomposition gives a contact-stage component (41.7 / 59.4 / 70.0 / 55.0 mm) larger than the motion-stage component (37.9 / 49.9 / 62.1 / 51.3 mm), whereas on the training subsample it is smaller (12.0 against 13.9 mm); the contact stage's test_1 / train ratio (3.46) is higher than the motion stage's (2.72), which is consistent with the contact stage generalising worse.
evidence.correction_reason: Pooled values, n and ratios confirmed (r1_paired_deltas.csv column scene; VERDICT_scene.json; recomputed from window_level.pkl). The pooled statement hides a hand asymmetry that is in the source tables (r1_split_hand_run.csv and r1_hand_asymmetry.csv, run=scene; the synthesis report J2 states that after the fix the left hand is the worse contact half on all four test splits). Without 'pooled over the two hands' the sentence reads as holding for the hands in general, which the table contradicts for the right hand. Same starting-noise caveat as the attribution.

evidence.claim: Between generation 1 and generation 3 of the TACO port (the scene-scale fix of the port's own contact-label scaling, which also changes the object input, with shorter training), the contact-stage component of the hand error on test_3 was lower by 30.38 mm [-34.61, -26.38] and the total hand error by 23.70 mm [-27.27, -20.14], while the motion-stage component changed by -3.63 mm [-6.20, -1.18] (paired over 1038 window-hands in 354 sequences, 95 % sequence-clustered bootstrap). test_3 is the largest effect; the contact-stage change on the other splits is -6.96, -7.40 and -12.26 mm. The gain is associated with the contact stage.
evidence.metric: Paired difference generation 3 minus generation 1 (scene - orig) of the per-window-hand stage components (contact_mm, motion_mm, total_mm as defined in the probe; mm; negative = improvement), over the same windows of a split. Interval = 95 % sequence-clustered paired bootstrap (2000 resamples, percentiles 2.5 / 97.5). test_3: n = 1038 window-hands (519 windows x 2 hands) in 354 sequences.

TACO | contact-stage delta gen3 - gen1,.locator: row split=test_3, metric=contact_mm, columns delta, lo, hi

TACO | contact-stage component, test_3:.locator: row split=test_3, metric=contact_mm, columns orig, scene

caveats: This is a BETWEEN-GENERATION delta (after minus before the label fix), not the gap between predicted-contact and ground-truth-contact conditioning. It shows that repairing the contact stage's label moved the hand error, mostly through the contact-stage component.

test_3 is the largest effect; the other splits are -6.96, -7.40 and -12.26 mm. test_3 is dominated by an unseen target category (305 of 354 sequences have a bowl target; 0 bowl targets in train; my count of sequence_index.csv).
The defect that was fixed was the port's own (scaling of the contact label), stated as such in the report ('The single largest fault was mine, not BimArt's').
The two generations also differ in the object input normalisation and in training length (200 / 200 against 110 / 60 epochs), not only in the label.
The predicted contact map's own error against its label did not improve (test_2 significantly worse); each generation is scored against its own label.
Generation-1 numbers can no longer be recomputed, only read off the frozen tables (INDEX.md).
Rounding in prose: scene_reverification.md prints the test_1 bounds as -4.16 and -11.37 where the CSV has -4.1545 and -11.3646.
evidence.claim_as_extracted: Correcting the contact stage's training label (generation 1 -> generation 3 of the TACO port) lowered the contact-stage component of the hand error on test_3 by 30.38 mm [-34.61, -26.38] and the total hand error by 23.70 mm [-27.27, -20.14], while the motion-stage component changed by -3.63 mm [-6.20, -1.18]: the gain is associated with the contact stage.
evidence.correction_reason: All values and intervals confirmed and the bootstrap reproduced exactly from window_level.pkl. 'Correcting the label lowered' attributes the change to the label alone, but the generations also differ in the scaled BPS object input, the scale entry of the global state and the training length (200 / 200 against 110 / 60 epochs), as the extractor's own caveat says. The claim quotes only the largest split. This is a between-generation delta about a defect of the port, not a predicted-versus-ground-truth contact gap, so it is weak evidence for the MOTIVATION message and must never be captioned as 'the contribution of contact to hand error'.

evidence.claim: For the released upstream BimArt on eight ARCTIC laptop test windows, the hand-keypoint RMSE is 22.4-126.4 mm with the ground-truth contact map and 68.2-322.7 mm with the contact stage's prediction, higher with the predicted map in every window, which is consistent with the contact stage contributing substantially to the hand error on BimArt's own data.
evidence.metric: total_mm = per-hand RMSE over the 100 keypoints of the distance between generated and recorded hand keypoints, averaged over 3 samples per arm, the 64 frames of a window and the two hands; mm, lower is better. Two arms with the same pretrained motion model (model_final.pth, epoch 199) and the same upstream inference procedure (conditioning, cost guidance, CFG 0.5): 'GT contact' versus 'stage-1 contact' (stage 1 re-sampled for every sample). Windows: the first 8 windows of BimArt's ARCTIC test split restricted to laptop (5 of laptop_grab_01_s01, 3 of laptop_use_04_s09). No interval stored.

ARCTIC | window selection.value: "restricted to {'laptop'}: 4 test files"; windows [1/8]..[8/8] = laptop_grab_01_s01_{100,164,228,292,356}, laptop_use_04_s09_{100,164,228}

caveats: Eight windows from two sequences of one object category (laptop), three samples per arm, no confidence interval: an illustration on BimArt's own data, not a split-level ARCTIC result.
Metric differs from the TACO table (per-hand RMSE here, mean keypoint distance there); levels are not comparable across the two datasets.
With the ground-truth map the hand is still 55.4-126.4 mm off on the five grab windows and 22.4-31.4 mm on the three use windows: the motion stage is not exonerated.
The ground-truth-contact arm is an oracle condition (map computed from the recorded hands); in this upstream path the contact map also drives the cost guidance, not only the conditioning.

No report prose exists for this ablation beyond the one-line README and the script docstring; the percentages 'share of the rigid shift removed by the GT map' (63-84 %) are plotted by the script (panel 4 of 01_contact_ablation.png, formula 100 * (1 - shift_GT / shift_stage1)) but are stored in no table. Quote mm values, or label any percentage as derived and as a share of the translation component, not of the hand error.
The run log lives in outputs/logs, which is git-ignored (not in the public repository).

do_not_claim: That -30.38 mm [-34.61, -26.38] is the cost of predicted contact relative to ground-truth contact, or 'the contribution of contact to hand error'. It is the generation-3 minus generation-1 change (the label fix) of the contact-stage component on TACO test_3.

That contact prediction 'causes 51-54 % of the hand error'. The table value is contact_mm / (motion_mm + contact_mm), a ratio of two near-orthogonal displacement magnitudes on 64 windows per split, TACO only, without an interval; it is not a fraction of the total and not a causal share.

Any percentage share obtained by subtracting the two evaluation columns (for example (58.6 - 37.1) / 58.6). The attribution script states that distances do not add linearly and that the subtraction is not the contact stage's share.
A single pooled or cross-dataset figure ('contact accounts for X % of hand error in hand-motion generation'), or any share for ARCTIC or OakInk2. None is stated in a source.

That contact generation is 'the' bottleneck or that it is 'proven'. The sources support 'a major source of downstream hand error': with the ground-truth map the motion stage is still 37-63 mm off on TACO test splits and 22-126 mm (RMSE) on the ARCTIC windows, and the report's own headline finding after the fix is take-level overfitting of the motion model plus the unseen-target-category frame effect.
That a better contact model would recover the whole gap. The ground-truth-contact arm is an oracle whose map is computed from the recorded hands.
That the ARCTIC result is a dataset-level or split-level measurement. It is 8 windows from 2 sequences of one object category, with no interval.

That the published BimArt fails on TACO or is a weak method. The TACO numbers are from this project's port (one training run, shorter training, test_1 used for validation), and the largest fault found was the port's own label scaling.
That BimArt -> OakInk2 shows the same thing. The OakInk2 models were never evaluated.

Any generation-1 or pre-fix number as the current state, in particular the table taco/15_bimart_gen1_inference_bughunt/ablation_ladder/evaluation/test_split_results.csv (72.5 / 86.7 mm on test_1), which INDEX.md and scene_reverification.md say must not be used for comparison; generation 2 is abandoned.
That the contact map prediction itself became more accurate after the label fix: the predicted map's error against its label did not improve (test_2: +3.21 mm [1.69, 4.70]).

A mix of the three window samples for the same model (128-window evaluation 58.6 / 86.5 / 104.9 / 79.8; all-window probe 60.1 / 85.5 / 99.4 / 79.9; 64-window attribution 59.8 / 95.9 / 113.1 / 85.7 mm) inside one comparison.
That the ARCTIC '63-84 % of the shift removed' is a share of the hand error or a stored result. It is plotted by the script from summary.json and concerns the rigid-translation component only.

page_headings: On TACO the amount of contact changes more within a take than between takes; the spatial layout changes less within a take than across meshes (TACO) or object instances (OakInk2), and only slightly less than across subjects on ARCTIC
source_labels: Dynamic contact representation · TACO / ARCTIC / OakInk2

figures.title: Contact amount and normalised spatial pattern: within-take change and identity change, relative to two takes

source_files.locator: column macro (n_groups, groups_gt_1 for the note); rows dataset in {TACO, ARCTIC, OakInk2}, (ratio, metric) = (time/take, mass_abs), (time/take, pattern_L2), and (mesh/take, pattern_L2) for TACO / OakInk2 or (subject/take_same_subject, pattern_L2) for ARCTIC
note only (no plotted value): row config = pattern_L2|mean|all|tol0.10; columns macro_subject_over_take, subject_gt_take, n_groups

figures.note: Each bar is a ratio of mean pair distances in one metric (amount = |difference of summed soft contact|, pattern = L2 between contact maps normalised to sum 1): early-vs-late frames of one take (time), or another mesh (TACO), object instance (OakInk2) or subject (ARCTIC) at matched phase, over two takes at matched phase; macro mean of per-group ratios, 1 = as different as two takes, no direction is better, no error bars (the tables give intervals per group only). Groups per bar (of which ratio > 1): TACO 8 (8), 8 (3), 8 (8); ARCTIC 22 (14), 22 (6), 22 (22); OakInk2 39 (2), 39 (0), 17 (16); the ARCTIC third bar divides by the same-subject cross-take distance, not by the denominator of its first two bars. Over the any-subject cross-take distance that its time bars use, the ARCTIC subject ratio of the pattern is 1.011 (16 of 22 groups above 1).

evidence.claim: On TACO, early and late frames of one take differ in contact amount about twice as much as two takes of the same mesh and verb at matched phase (time/take 2.12, above 1 in 8 of 8 groups), while their normalised spatial pattern differs about as much as between two such takes (time/take 1.04, above 1 in 3 of 8 groups); a different mesh at matched phase changes the pattern more than a different take does (mesh/take 1.48, 8 of 8 groups), and the within-take pattern change stays below the mesh-to-mesh difference in every group (time/mesh 0.69, 0 of 8 groups above 1).
evidence.metric: Unitless ratio of two mean pair distances of the SAME metric inside one group (category x role x hand): numerator = pairs along one axis, denominator = pairs of two different takes of the same mesh and verb at matched phase (phase difference < 0.10). time = two frames of one take with phase difference > 0.5 (early vs late); mesh = other mesh, same verb, matched phase. amount = |difference of mass|, mass = sum of the 512-D soft contact map (soft = exp(-d / 2 cm)); pattern = L2 distance between maps normalised to sum 1 (defined only when neither frame is zero-contact). Headline = macro (unweighted mean of the 8 per-group ratios), mean over pairs. 1 = as different as two takes at the same phase; no direction is better. Experiment 1 of the dynamic-contact study; frames = every 2nd frame of 64-frame windows with touch fraction >= 0.2; up to 4000 cross pairs per group and axis, 3074-13369 time pairs per group.

caveats: The two ratios are in different metrics, each divided by its own cross-take level; '2.12 vs 1.04' is a comparison relative to take-to-take variation, not an absolute amount-versus-pattern comparison.

Pattern time/take is 1.036 as a macro mean but 0.964 pooled, and three of eight groups (spoon, roller, knife; all tool / right hand) are 1.3-1.5: say 'about the same as between two takes', not 'smaller than between takes'.
The macro values have no confidence interval in the sources; intervals exist per group only (95 % paired sequence-level bootstrap, 500 replicates).
'Mesh' on TACO is confounded with subject / session (report: tool meshes are used by 1-6 subjects, mean 2.1): the mesh ratio is 'the mesh and whoever used it', not pure geometry.

Phase is the position inside the touching span of a take, not an alignment of task events; 'time' means early vs late (phase difference > 0.5) inside takes of 64-448 windowed frames (median 128 = 4.3 s).
No grasp label exists in this study: the axes are take, mesh, action (verb); 'grasp identity' is not measured here.
Statement is about 512-D canonical contact maps only, not about hand motion.

evidence.claim: On ARCTIC, where a take lasts 18-37 s, early and late frames of one take differ in normalised spatial pattern slightly less than two takes do (time/take 0.94, above 1 in 6 of 22 groups); in contact amount they differ about as much on |delta mass| (1.10, 14 of 22 groups) and more on log-mass (1.57, 22 of 22), and that excess is associated with pairs in which one frame is zero-contact (0.90 and 0.98 when neither frame is zero-contact); frames from a different subject differ in pattern 1.16 times the same-subject cross-take level (22 of 22 groups), which is 1.01 times the any-subject cross-take level that the time ratio uses (16 of 22 groups).
evidence.metric: Same ratio definition as TACO, group = (object, hand), 22 groups, macro mean of per-group ratios, 1 = cross-take level, no direction is better. ARCTIC has one mesh per object, so the identity axis is the SUBJECT: 'subject' = other subject, same verb; the table divides it by 'take_same_subject' (same subject, other take, same verb), NOT by the 'take' level (other take, same verb, any subject) that time/take uses.

caveats: The subject ratio 1.16 is over the SAME-SUBJECT cross-take level; against the take level used by the time ratios the subject ratio is 1.011. Do not draw both against one unlabelled reference line.

Takes are 512-1088 windowed frames (median 704 = 23.5 s) and contain several contact episodes; 17 % of frames are zero-contact. A phase gap of 0.5 is at least 10 s here against 1-2 s on TACO, so phase-based ratios are on a coarser time scale (report caveat).
On |delta mass| the temporal excess is weak (1.10, 14 of 22 groups); the strong value (1.57) is the log-mass metric, which is sensitive to on/off pairs.
Few within-take pairs: 473-612 time pairs per group (4000 for the cross axes), hence wide per-group intervals.
One mesh per object: nothing here tests geometry; the subject axis is confounded with session and hand size (report caveat).
The ARCTIC report states that on articulated objects amount and pattern grow together in the lag curves ('the location drifts with the amount'); the simple TACO picture is weakest here.
evidence.claim_as_extracted: On ARCTIC, where a take lasts 18-37 s, early and late frames of one take differ in normalised spatial pattern slightly less than two takes do (time/take 0.94, above 1 in 6 of 22 groups) and in contact amount about as much (1.10 on |delta mass|, 14 of 22 groups; 1.57 on log-mass, 22 of 22), and that amount excess is associated with pairs in which one frame has no contact (0.90 and 0.98 once both frames are in contact); a different subject changes the pattern 1.16 times the same-subject cross-take level (22 of 22 groups).
evidence.correction_reason: Every number is confirmed. Three wording fixes: 1.57 is not 'about as much'; 'in contact' should be 'neither frame zero-contact' (the both_nonzero variant; zero = mass < 4.0 and no vertex within 1 cm); and the subject ratio must carry its like-for-like value 1.011 in the same sentence, otherwise 1.16 is read against the 0.94 time ratio, which has a different denominator.

evidence.claim: On OakInk2, whose takes are interaction-only segments without approach and retreat, early and late frames of one take differ less than two takes do on both the amount (time/take 0.60, above 1 in 2 of 39 groups) and the normalised spatial pattern (0.45, 0 of 39 groups), while frames from a different object instance of the same category differ in pattern 1.69 times the cross-take level (16 of the 17 groups that have this axis); in a control run with the annotated approach and retreat included (39 common groups, a larger take sample), the amount ratio is above 1 (1.38 against 0.60; 33 against 2 groups above 1) and the pattern ratio is higher but still below 1 (0.61 against 0.45; 2 against 0 groups).
evidence.metric: Same ratio definition, group = (category, hand), macro mean of per-group ratios; 39 groups for time/take, 17 groups for mesh/take (groups where two instances share a verb). take = other take, same instance and verb, matched phase (subject free); mesh = other instance of the category, same verb. 1 = cross-take level; no direction is better.

The last clause reads as an intervention on identical takes, but the two runs contain different take samples (1,985 against 3,239 takes in the 39 common groups, because the interaction-only index lost 1,780 rows without a frame count); state it as a comparison of two runs. evidence.claim: On each of the three datasets the early-vs-late difference of the normalised spatial pattern within a take is near or below the take-to-take difference (time/take 1.04 on TACO, 0.94 on ARCTIC, 0.45 on OakInk2), and an identity axis exceeds its own cross-take reference (mesh/take 1.48 on TACO; object-instance/take 1.69 on OakInk2, over 17 of 39 groups; on ARCTIC subject over same-subject take 1.16, which is 1.01 against the any-subject take level used by the time ratio). The amount ordering across datasets (2.12, 1.10, 0.60) follows how much approach, release and on/off each take contains, as the reports and the OakInk2 control state; it is not a statement about the datasets' objects.

The cross-dataset narrative's sentence 'whatever temporal excess exists is amount, not location' sits beside an ARCTIC report that marks the lag structure as a NOT-same conclusion (amount and pattern grow together on articulated objects) and an OakInk2 report that calls the residual within-take change 'spatial re-adjustment as much as amount'.
The table 'OakInk2-ext' column of the cross-dataset report is over all 65 extended groups (time/take amount 1.3596); the control comparison over the 39 common groups gives 1.3819.

evidence.claim_as_extracted: Across the three datasets the within-take change of the normalised spatial pattern is near or below the take-to-take difference (time/take 1.04 TACO, 0.94 ARCTIC, 0.45 OakInk2) while an identity axis is above it (mesh 1.48 on TACO, subject 1.16 over the same-subject take level on ARCTIC, object instance 1.69 on OakInk2); whether the amount shows a temporal excess depends on how a take is cut (2.12 on TACO takes with approach and release, 1.10 on long multi-episode ARCTIC takes, 0.60 on interaction-only OakInk2 segments).
evidence.correction_reason: Values confirmed. Two problems in the wording: (1) 'an identity axis is above it' puts ARCTIC's 1.16 against the take-to-take level, but its denominator is the same-subject take level; against the take level it is 1.011 (16 of 22 groups). (2) 'depends on how a take is cut' is a causal statement across datasets that differ in many other ways; the only direct evidence is the OakInk2 control, which also changes the take sample. Use 'differs in line with' and 'is consistent with'.

evidence.claim: The temporal excess of the amount is associated with pairs in which at least one frame has low or zero contact: on TACO the amount time/take is 0.94 when both frames are at or above the group-median amount (4 of 8 groups above 1) but 1.44 when both frames have a vertex within 1 cm (6 of 8), and the pattern ratio is below 1 under both restrictions (0.65 and 0.80); on ARCTIC the amount ratio is 0.90 (|delta mass|) and 0.98 (log-mass) when neither frame is zero-contact. The reports read this as approach / release grading on TACO and as on/off between contact episodes on ARCTIC.
evidence.metric: Macro time/take ratio (mean over pairs, phase tolerance 0.10, touching windows) recomputed on restricted pair sets: both_nonzero (neither frame zero-contact), high_contact (both frames at or above the group-median mass), both_hard (both frames have an object vertex within 1 cm of the hand). 1 = cross-take level; no direction is better.
caveats: Keep both TACO restrictions: 'the time excess disappears in firm contact' holds for the above-median restriction (0.94) and not for the 1 cm rule (1.44).
On TACO the excess is hovering-to-firm-contact grading, not on/off (at most 6.6 % of time pairs have one zero frame); on ARCTIC it is on/off (22-36 % of time pairs). The mechanisms differ by dataset.
Soft contact has a long tail (a hand hovering 4 cm away still gives about 0.13 per vertex), so 'amount' includes near-contact, not only touching.
These restricted values are from the verification table (float32 recomputation; they differ from ratios.csv in the 8th digit).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: The temporal excess of the amount is associated with approach / release and on-off phases of a take: on TACO it disappears when both frames are above the group-median amount (time/take 0.94) but remains 1.44 when both frames merely have a vertex within 1 cm, and in both restrictions the pattern ratio is below 1 (0.65 and 0.80); on ARCTIC it disappears once both frames are in contact.
evidence.correction_reason: Numbers confirmed in the two verify tables. Approach and release phases are not labelled on TACO or ARCTIC; the restrictions select pairs by contact amount, so 'associated with approach / release phases' is the reports' interpretation, not the measured condition. 'Disappears' for 0.94 hides that 4 of 8 groups are still above 1. ARCTIC values should be stated, and 'in contact' means 'neither frame zero-contact'.

evidence.claim: Secondary (lag structure): within a take the normalised pattern does change with time lag on every dataset; at about 1 s (lag 32 frames) it reaches 0.67 of the cross-take level on TACO, 0.54 on ARCTIC and 0.25 on OakInk2, against 1.28, 0.56 and 0.32 for the amount, so the amount outruns the pattern on TACO while the two grow together on ARCTIC and OakInk2.
evidence.metric: Experiment 2: mean distance between frames t and t + lag of one take (frames at 30 fps, 'touching' set = both frames non-zero, per-take means), divided by the group's matched-phase cross-take distance of the same metric; macro over groups. 1 = cross-take level. 'top-10 % share' = fraction of a take's summed frame-to-frame change carried by its 10 % largest frames, against an iid half-normal null. No direction is better.

Small predictors, one MLP and one ridge, no per-condition hyper-parameter search, fold seeds only; training sets outside TACO are small, so the weaker predictability on ARCTIC and OakInk2 is partly a data-size statement.
OakInk2: 'none on average'; the report says the object state helps in most of the larger groups and hurts in the small ones.
Nothing here measures whether a better contact representation improves the hand-motion stage (stated by the TACO report).

do_not_claim: 'Contact does not move over time' or 'the spatial pattern is constant within a take': the pattern changes with lag on all three datasets, exceeds the take level in 3 of 8 TACO groups and 6 of 22 ARCTIC groups, and the reports show a migrating take.
'Within a take the spatial pattern varies less than between takes' as a general statement: true on OakInk2 (0.45), marginal on ARCTIC (0.94), not true on TACO as a macro mean (1.04; pooled 0.96).
'On all datasets the amount changes much more over time than the pattern': only TACO shows it (2.12 vs 1.04); ARCTIC 1.10 vs 0.94, OakInk2 0.60 vs 0.45 with both below the take level.
That the amount ratio and the pattern ratio are directly comparable magnitudes: they are different metrics, each divided by its own cross-take level.
'Grasp identity changes the pattern': no grasp label or grasp axis exists in this study; the measured axes are take, mesh / object instance, subject and action (verb).
'Geometry changes the pattern by 1.48x' as a pure geometry effect: TACO meshes are confounded with the subjects who used them; on ARCTIC the subject axis is confounded with session and hand size.
A single 'subject/take' number comparable across ARCTIC and OakInk2: ARCTIC's 1.16 is over the same-subject take level, OakInk2's 1.07 over the any-subject take level.
'The temporal amount excess disappears in firm contact' without the second number: on TACO it is 0.94 above median mass but 1.44 under the 1 cm hard-contact rule.
Any confidence interval or significance statement for the macro ratios: the sources give bootstrap intervals per group only.
That OakInk2 was analysed on 4,603 takes: 1,985 takes entered the analysis.
That the OakInk2 control isolates the effect of approach and retreat on identical takes: the two runs contain different take samples (1,985 vs 3,239 takes in the common groups).
A pooled or averaged cross-dataset ratio: none exists in the sources and none should be computed.
That these ratios show time is 'irrelevant' or 'noise', or that a static contact map is sufficient: the ARCTIC report states that one static map per take is not enough on long articulated takes.
That this study shows a better contact representation improves hand-motion generation: the TACO report says it does not measure that.
Causal wording such as 'approach and release cause the amount change': the sources show an association through pair restrictions and one control, not an intervention on the same takes.

caveats: Best-of-K is an oracle: the sample is picked with the ground truth of the whole rollout. It shows that a good initial map is among K samples, not that the generator finds it.
B0 and B1 use the TRUE first contact map; they are diagnostic rows, not generators. 'Static persistence 3.48' is the true s_0 held for 64 frames.
Raw E_C units differ between datasets (contact-mass scales differ): compare within a dataset, never raw values across datasets.

One training seed (0) and one fixed split per dataset. TACO test = the dataset's test_1 (every group, mesh and subject also occurs in training). ARCTIC test = 44 takes, OakInk2 test = 34 recordings, so intervals are wide.
The evolution is deterministic by construction (one vector field, free Euler rollout); this experiment did not compare it with a stochastic evolution.
The object trajectory is a given input, and the local context of the vector field includes object states up to 8 frames ahead.
G is the static condition: per-mesh surface descriptor at the 512 canonical points, mesh radius and extent, and one-hot hand and role flags (so 'geometry-only' includes which hand and which role).
With one sample (K=1) the generator is above the static true-s_0 row on ARCTIC (3.70 vs 2.21) and OakInk2 (4.09 vs 1.26); only on TACO is it below (2.59 vs 3.48).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: Generating a 64-frame contact sequence as 'sample an initial contact map s_0 from object geometry, then evolve it deterministically with the object motion' is supported on TACO, where both stages contribute; on ARCTIC and OakInk2 the evolution stage provides little additional information beyond holding the true s_0 and the error is dominated by the choice of s_0.

(2) 'both stages contribute' on TACO rests, for the sampler, on the oracle best-of-10; that caveat has to sit in the sentence. 'Little additional information' on ARCTIC hides a wide interval (-0.257 to +0.107): 'no measurable benefit' is the accurate strength. G also includes one-hot hand and role flags (data.py).

do_not_claim: 'Sample-then-evolve works on all three datasets' or 'temporal evolution halves the error' as a general statement: the evolution benefit is a TACO result; on ARCTIC and OakInk2 it is not distinguishable from holding the true first map.
'Ten samples match the ground-truth initialisation' as a general statement: it holds on TACO only (+0.036, interval contains zero); ARCTIC +0.339 and OakInk2 +1.270 are significantly above.

'The generator reaches 1.86' or any wording that presents best-of-10 as a deployable result: best-of-K is selected with the ground truth of the whole rollout (oracle). The single-sample numbers are 2.59 (TACO), 3.70 (ARCTIC), 4.09 (OakInk2).

'The multimodality lives entirely in s_0' (the report's own phrase) or 'all the multimodality is in the initial contact': the tables support 'a large part of the multimodality is associated with the initial contact / grasp-mode selection', no more.

'The future is deterministic given s_0', 'deterministic evolution is sufficient / optimal / necessary' or 'universally deterministic': this experiment used only a deterministic vector field and never compared it with a stochastic evolution; on ARCTIC that deterministic evolution does not beat holding s_0.

'Contact does not move over time on ARCTIC / OakInk2': on ARCTIC 42 % of the test sequences leave firm contact within the window and the static pattern error is 0.0417; the null there is a failure to predict the change, not absence of change.
'Static persistence (3.48) is a naive baseline': it holds the TRUE first contact map, which a generator does not have.

'The learned sampler predicts the grasp' or 'is an accurate initial-contact model': a single sample is about as far from the truth as a random real training take, and FURTHER than the mean training map of the mesh on every dataset (2.350 vs 1.865; 2.395 vs 1.951; 4.122 vs 3.346).
'Object motion selects the grasp mode': adding motion context to the sampler helps one sample on TACO / ARCTIC but makes best-of-10 equal or worse on every dataset.

'The evolution models contact dynamics frame by frame': its frame-to-frame error is no better than a constant map on TACO / OakInk2 and worse on ARCTIC; the TACO gain is in the slow contact-amount trend.
'The evolution is always safe to apply': from a single sampled map on ARCTIC it is significantly worse than holding that map (+0.245 [+0.068, +0.436]).
'Generalises to unseen objects': the main TACO test contains only seen groups / meshes / subjects; on the two TACO groups with no training take the evolution is worse than static.
Any cross-dataset comparison or average of raw E_C values, or a pooled 'mean improvement over datasets'.
Any statement of robustness across seeds or splits: one training seed and one fixed split per dataset.
'Grasp intent', 'human intention' or named grasp modes: the experiment has no mode labels; 'mode' means the spread of first-contact maps across takes of the same object and hand.

'The best-of-10 rollout was compared with the same sample held static': at best-of-10 the held-static row uses its own best sample (chosen by held-static error); only the K=1 comparison uses literally the same sample.

caveats: The share of transitions is close to 10 % by construction: the threshold is the per-dataset TRAIN 90th percentile, so '12.6 % / 5.7 % / 9.3 % of transitions' is not a discovered sparsity; the finding is the energy share. 'Spike' means large for that dataset (thresholds 0.616 / 0.564 / 0.292 raw units), so absolute d_t is not comparable across datasets.

Squaring emphasises large changes: in unsquared magnitude the spikes hold 39 % / 29 % / 35 %, and the report's own wording is 'concentrated but not sparse' (the remaining 28-38 % of the change energy is a floor of small changes on non-spike frames).

Not every spike is a lasting reconfiguration: 46 % (TACO) and 53 % (OakInk2) of the events are low-persistence (the change cancels out within +-4 frames) against 7 % on ARCTIC, and a 3-frame moving average keeps only 28 % / 46 % of the spike energy on TACO / OakInk2 (63 % on ARCTIC). The report states it cannot decide whether these are real micro-adjustments or tracking jitter.

Test split of the fixed split only (TACO test_1; ARCTIC test; OakInk2 seeded 80/10/10 by recording); 64-frame windows that start at the first firm-contact frame; analysis of cached sequences, nothing retrained.
The report prose rounds the energy shares to 70 % / 62 % / 72 %; the tables give 0.697 / 0.624 / 0.721.

evidence.claim: What the large changes are differs by dataset. By event count, TACO and OakInk2 spike events are mostly mixed or spatial-dominant (TACO 59 % and 28 % of events; OakInk2 55 % and 39 %). On ARCTIC mixed events are 48 % of the events, and firm-contact onset / release events are 26 % of the events and carry 46 % of the spike energy (wide intervals, 44 takes). At the canonical 0.7 / 0.3 cut amount-dominant events are a minority in each dataset - 4.9 % (TACO), 14.1 % (ARCTIC) and 4.7 % (OakInk2) of events, 2.8 % / 5.0 % / 1.9 % of the spike energy - but on ARCTIC that share depends on the cut (30 % of events at 0.6 / 0.4).
evidence.metric: Adjacent spike transitions merged into events. Event type, in priority order: onset / release / onset+release if the event contains a firm-contact transition; otherwise amount-dominant (amount ratio r >= 0.7), spatial-dominant (r <= 0.3) or mixed, with r from the exact decomposition dC = dm * P_bar + m_bar * dP aggregated over the event. Reported: share of events (frequency) and share of the spike-frame sum d_t^2 (energy) with a take-level cluster-bootstrap 95 % interval on the energy share. Descriptive, no better direction.

do_not_claim: 'Temporal failure (the temporal error) is concentrated in spatial / mixed transitions' as a statement about the total error: 61-77 % of every B0-B3 model's summed temporal error is on NON-spike frames (B1: 64 % / 77 % / 66 %).

'The temporal model's gains are in the slow evolution' as a per-class result: the per-class comparison is on spike frames only; on non-spike frames the evolved model's temporal error is not lower than static (ARCTIC: higher). The 'slow amount trend' reading is the report's interpretation of the TACO absolute-error gain and is TACO-only.

'The model predicts amount changes well' or 'the model perfectly predicts sliding': on TACO amount frames it still has 0.685 against 0.877 for static, and on spatial-dominant frames it is unchanged on every dataset.
'The model cannot predict any spatial or mixed change': mixed frames are lower on TACO (0.992 -> 0.917) and ARCTIC (0.825 -> 0.763).
'The evolved model beats the static baseline in temporal error': averaged over all transitions it does not (0.317 vs 0.318; 0.167 vs 0.194; 0.142 vs 0.144).
Any ARCTIC or OakInk2 per-class difference presented as significant: their B0 / B1 intervals overlap and no paired test exists in this thread.

'Only about 10 % of frames matter' or '12.6 % of frames' as a discovered sparsity: the threshold is the train 90th percentile, so the frame share is near 10 % by construction; the report's own conclusion is 'concentrated but not sparse'.
A pooled statement such as 'about 10 % of transitions hold about 70 % of the change' across datasets: report 12.6 % -> 69.7 % (TACO), 5.7 % -> 62.4 % (ARCTIC), 9.3 % -> 72.1 % (OakInk2) separately.

'Spikes are sliding / regrasp / reconfiguration events': on TACO and OakInk2 about half of the events are low-persistence oscillations that cancel within a few frames, and the report cannot tell real micro-adjustments from tracking jitter. Equally do not call them 'noise' or 'jitter' as a fact (the report's phrase 'treat the residual high-frequency part as noise' is a recommendation for a training target, not a finding).
'Contact does not move over time' or 'spatial changes are irrelevant': nothing in this thread supports either.
'Hand motion predicts (or causes, or drives) contact change': the Spearman values are same-transition associations; the follow-up study found the coupling mostly simultaneous.

'Object motion is unrelated to contact change': the correlations are weak (0.01-0.33), not zero; OakInk2's object angular speed is 0.333 and on TACO object / tool speeds are elevated during spatial and mixed events.
Quoting 0.68 as the TACO hand correlation without the correction, or quoting TACO's Cliff's delta 0.70 / 'median hand speed triples' as corrected values (they were not recomputed).
Any hand-motion statement for OakInk2 (no hand signal), or 'hand-relative speed is the strongest signal on all three datasets'.

Describing the timeline as 'ground-truth versus predicted contact change': the table holds the error of the predicted change, not its magnitude; and the two sequences are single illustrations, not typical-case statistics.
Attributing the TACO BimArt (B4) numbers to the released BimArt model, or comparing BimArt 'own support' errors with B0 / B1 as like-for-like.
Using the report's hypothesis letters (A-D): A and C are never defined in the saved files.
Presenting the report's recommendation (train on a 3-5 frame smoothed / persistent displacement) as a tested result: it was not tested in this thread.
'Amount-dominant changes are rare' as cut-independent on ARCTIC (30 % of events at the 0.6/0.4 cut).

'The model predicts amount changes well' or 'the model perfectly predicts sliding': on TACO amount frames it still has 0.685 against 0.877 for static, and on spatial-dominant frames it is unchanged on every dataset.
'The model cannot predict any spatial or mixed change': mixed frames are lower on TACO (0.992 -> 0.917) and ARCTIC (0.825 -> 0.763).
'The evolved model beats the static baseline in temporal error': averaged over all transitions it does not (0.317 vs 0.318; 0.167 vs 0.194; 0.142 vs 0.144).
Any ARCTIC or OakInk2 per-class difference presented as significant: their B0 / B1 intervals overlap and no paired test exists in this thread.

'Only about 10 % of frames matter' or '12.6 % of frames' as a discovered sparsity: the threshold is the train 90th percentile, so the frame share is near 10 % by construction; the report's own conclusion is 'concentrated but not sparse'.
A pooled statement such as 'about 10 % of transitions hold about 70 % of the change' across datasets: report 12.6 % -> 69.7 % (TACO), 5.7 % -> 62.4 % (ARCTIC), 9.3 % -> 72.1 % (OakInk2) separately.

'Spikes are sliding / regrasp / reconfiguration events': on TACO and OakInk2 about half of the events are low-persistence oscillations that cancel within a few frames, and the report cannot tell real micro-adjustments from tracking jitter. Equally do not call them 'noise' or 'jitter' as a fact (the report's phrase 'treat the residual high-frequency part as noise' is a recommendation for a training target, not a finding).
'Contact does not move over time' or 'spatial changes are irrelevant': nothing in this thread supports either.
'Hand motion predicts (or causes, or drives) contact change': the Spearman values are same-transition associations; the follow-up study found the coupling mostly simultaneous.

'Object motion is unrelated to contact change': the correlations are weak (0.01-0.33), not zero; OakInk2's object angular speed is 0.333 and on TACO object / tool speeds are elevated during spatial and mixed events.
Quoting 0.68 as the TACO hand correlation without the correction, or quoting TACO's Cliff's delta 0.70 / 'median hand speed triples' as corrected values (they were not recomputed).
Any hand-motion statement for OakInk2 (no hand signal), or 'hand-relative speed is the strongest signal on all three datasets'.

Describing the timeline as 'ground-truth versus predicted contact change': the table holds the error of the predicted change, not its magnitude; and the two sequences are single illustrations, not typical-case statistics.
Attributing the TACO BimArt (B4) numbers to the released BimArt model, or comparing BimArt 'own support' errors with B0 / B1 as like-for-like.
Using the report's hypothesis letters (A-D): A and C are never defined in the saved files.
Presenting the report's recommendation (train on a 3-5 frame smoothed / persistent displacement) as a tested result: it was not tested in this thread.
'Amount-dominant changes are rare' as cut-independent on ARCTIC (30 % of events at the 0.6/0.4 cut).

evidence.claim: On held-out test transitions the size of the frame-to-frame contact change is associated with the hand's speed relative to the contacted object: Spearman 0.785 [0.767, 0.801] on TACO (22,932 transitions) and 0.513 [0.413, 0.621] on ARCTIC (11,718). This same-step association, stronger on TACO than on ARCTIC, is what motivated asking whether the hand also predicts the change ahead of time.
evidence.metric: Spearman rank correlation between d_t = ||C_{t+1} - C_t|| (one-step contact change) and the speed of the hand relative to the contacted object, over test transitions; interval = take-cluster bootstrap (200 replicates in build_hand_cache.py). Higher = stronger same-frame association; it is not a prediction score.
caveats: This is a same-transition association (hand speed and contact change at the same step), not predictive information.
The TACO value uses the tool-frame transform corrected in this study; the earlier temporal-event report gives 0.68 for the same quantity.
It is a sanity statistic of the cache build, not one of the study's designed comparisons.
ARCTIC's interval is wide (44 takes in the test set).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: On held-out test transitions the size of the frame-to-frame contact change is strongly associated with the hand's speed relative to the object (Spearman 0.78 on TACO, 0.51 on ARCTIC); this association is why the study asks whether the hand also predicts the change ahead of time.
evidence.correction_reason: Values confirmed. 'Strongly' fits TACO; ARCTIC's 0.51 with an interval down to 0.41 does not carry the same adjective. Use 0.785 for TACO: the report and INDEX print 0.79, the extractor 0.78, and the cell is 0.7848. It is a sanity statistic of the cache build (200 take-bootstrap replicates), same-step, not a prediction score. The motivating earlier report printed 0.68 for TACO (wrong tool-frame transform).

The shuffled-hand control lowers AUPRC below the no-hand classifier on both datasets (an uninformative 2700-D input costs the small MLP something); measured against that control the real hand history is worth +0.082 AUPRC on TACO and +0.011 (n.s.) on ARCTIC.
Per-condition intervals overlap between neighbouring bars although some paired differences exclude 0; the paired table is the test.
The report's 'recall at precision 0.5 <= 0.23 / 0.03 for every causal model' holds at h = 4 only; at h = 8 TACO's no-hand classifier already reaches recall 0.50 at precision 0.5.
ARCTIC intervals are wide (44 takes, 677 positive frames at h = 4); absolute AUPRC values are low (prevalence 6-17 %).
One future frame does not help this task (oracle +1: 0.372 TACO, 0.118 ARCTIC at h = 4); no paired row oracle +1 vs no hand exists.

On the squared error (the training criterion) ARCTIC's point estimates are positive (no hand 1.3 %, history 7.6 %, motion-only 13.2 %, oracle 33.9 %), with intervals that exclude 0 only for motion-only and the oracle.

do_not_claim: Hand motion is irrelevant to (or independent of) contact change: the same-step association is strong (Spearman 0.78 TACO / 0.51 ARCTIC) and the future-hand oracle shows the information exists.
The hand causes, or does not cause, contact change: 'causal' here means only that the input uses hand frames at or before the current frame; nothing was intervened on.

Causal hand history carries no information / gives no gain: the gains are small but several have intervals that exclude 0 (TACO beyond the shuffled control; release, onset and persistent mixed frames on both datasets).

The past hand cannot predict transition timing at all, or transition timing is unpredictable: on TACO the causal inputs add a small significant AUPRC gain (+0.03) and the no-hand model is already far above chance (0.332 vs 0.098).
'10-28 % on release' as a result for both datasets or against one baseline: it is a TACO range mixing 'vs no hand' and 'vs shuffled control'; ARCTIC is 6.6-17.6 %.
'Causal history gives 2-7 %' as an ARCTIC statement without the control: ARCTIC's range is 2.1-4.2 % and its absolute-history gain equals the shuffled control in mean L2.
A single pooled number such as 'the oracle helps by about 17 %': report TACO (-17.7 %) and ARCTIC (-15.6 %) separately.
The oracle shows what a hand-contact co-evolution model would achieve: it uses ground-truth future hands and is an upper bound on information; generated hands were never tested.
Hand and contact are simultaneous, stated as an established mechanism: the tables are consistent with a largely simultaneous coupling (the report's 'Case D' reading).
Persistent spatial contact changes are unexplained by the hand in general: on TACO the +8 oracle removes 24.9 % and the causal inputs 4-6 %; the null is ARCTIC's.
On ARCTIC the +8 oracle beats predicting no change: its improvement interval includes 0; and every causal ARCTIC predictor is worse than predicting no change in mean L2.
The current hand pose makes prediction worse, as a robust effect: it is the 3-seed mean on TACO, reversed in one seed, and absent on ARCTIC; and the pose is what helps the TACO transition classifier.

Dynamics matter, static configuration does not, as a general law: it was measured with one architecture and one hand representation (100 surface points, flattened), with exceptions listed in the caveats.
The hypotheses or decision cases were pre-registered: no plan file exists for this study; say 'the hypotheses and decision cases stated in the report'.
The oracle +1 bar has a confidence interval or a paired test against the no-hand model: no such row exists; the value is the sum of two paired rows.
Overlapping per-condition error bars in the AUPRC figure mean 'no difference' (or non-overlap means a significant difference): the paired differences are the test.
The gain is confined to release / onset / mixed frames: on TACO the motion-only input also lowers the error on quiet frames (-7.7 %).

The Figure F example panels are representative: per dataset they are the two events where the 8-frame history helped most and the two where it hurt most, from seed-0 models; they are dense research panels with internal labels and are not page-ready.
Any OakInk2 statement for this block.
The 'No-Go for co-evolution' is an experimental result: it is the report's design decision drawn from these numbers.

evidence.claim: For persistent spatial contact events inside a firmly held grasp (TACO 119 events, ARCTIC 26), the grasp before the event already holds most of the modelled wrench capability of the grasp after it (median pre→post retention 0.85 on TACO and 0.89 on ARCTIC, median profile cosine 0.97 / 0.96, median relative change of the direction-averaged capability +0.04 / +0.02), which supports reading many of these dense reconfigurations as preserving a wrench-capability proxy for functional grasp capability, under the modelled constraints.
evidence.metric: Per event: PRE grasp (frame before the event) versus POST grasp (frame after it), each built from the contact at its own frame in the object frame (no transport). Capability profile = support-function capacity h(u) along 76 shared 6-D force/torque directions (64 random, fixed seed, + 12 signed axes) of a contact-patch model (unit force budget per finger and palm, 8-edge Coulomb cone with mu = 0.5, torque divided by the object size); normalised units, not newtons. Retention pre→post = mean over directions of min(h_pre / h_post, 1): 1 = the PRE grasp already had all of the POST grasp's capability (one-sided). Profile cosine = cosine similarity of the two 76-D profiles (1 = same shape; blind to an overall scale change). Relative change = (Q_post − Q_pre) / Q_pre with Q = mean of the profile (0 = unchanged). Table values are MEDIANS over test-split events; intervals are 95 % percentile intervals of a bootstrap that resamples whole takes (1 000 replicates). Neither direction is 'better': values near 1 (retention, cosine) or 0 (relative change) mean the capability is preserved.

caveats: Wrench capability is a modelled PROXY in normalised units (unit finger budgets, linearised Coulomb friction, torque normalised by object size, mesh centroid as torque origin). Object mass, centre of mass, inertia, hand force limits and friction are unavailable in both datasets; this is not a physical feasibility result and says nothing about why the fingers moved (report section 12).

The values are MEDIANS over events, not a statement about every event: 20 % (TACO) / 23 % (ARCTIC) gain more than 25 % and 8 / 3 events lose more than 25 %; only 34 % / 46 % of events retain at least 0.9. The report's own verdict is 'heterogeneous with a dominant function-preserving pattern' ('Case C with a strong Case-A component').

Retention is one-sided by design: a grasp that shrank scores close to 1 (a release scores exactly 1). Quote it together with the reverse retention (0.91 / 0.89), the cosine or the relative change. The report's phrase 'retains 85–90 % of the post grasp's capability in every direction' is loose: it is a mean over directions of a capped ratio, not a per-direction guarantee.

The 0.85 / 0.89 are specific to the single-hand support-function measure (other wrench components assumed balanced by the other hand / table / tool contact). Under the strict exact-direction measure the median retention is 0.66 [0.33, 0.78] (TACO) / 0.75 [0.11, 0.92] (ARCTIC).

TACO shows a small but systematic gain rather than exactly zero: lower CI bound of the median relative change 0.0037 > 0, mean +0.13 [0.07, 0.21], Q_post > Q_pre in 63 % of events (the report attributes it to a slightly larger post grasp). On ARCTIC the interval of the median straddles zero [−0.09, +0.19].
ARCTIC is small: 26 events from 15 takes; its intervals are wide (retention [0.76, 0.96]).

'Persistent spatial' is a minority class defined by two labelled cuts of the earlier event analysis (amount ratio ≤ 0.3; persistence over ±4 frames ≥ 0.5; firm contact before, after and throughout): 123 (119 analysed) of 1 464 detected TACO test events and 26 of 283 on ARCTIC. The larger persistent mixed class (452 / 131) behaves differently. The claim is about this class, not about post-grasp reconfigurations in general.

Events are short: PRE and POST are 1 frame apart in the median TACO event and 2 in the median ARCTIC event (events.csv post_frame − pre_frame; max 13 / 9), so a 'reconfiguration' is a contact-map jump between nearby frames that then persists.
Reference level: the diagnostic transient (frame-jitter) class has retention 0.90 / 0.94, so the persistent spatial class is only slightly below it.

Correction of the task text: retention and cosine do NOT use a transported pre grasp. Each grasp is evaluated at its own frame in the object frame (wrench_analysis.py: geom_dict(g, 'pre') / geom_dict(g, 'post')). Transport by mesh vertex id is used only for the future-motion directions.
The word 'missed' in the block title rests on another report (hand_contact_predictive_info_report.md lines 24–26: 'least explained'); this study measures no prediction error.
OakInk2 is excluded from this study (no hand geometry in the object frame in its caches).

Stale sentences in the report's Limitations section ('TACO's 100 analysed persistent-spatial events ... 61 takes'; 'ARCTIC ... 26 ... (37 takes)') contradict every table (119 / 73 and 26 / 15). The report's '177 / 37 test takes' are takes with at least one detected event; the fixed test split has 186 / 44 takes.

evidence.claim: Events that change the contact amount are associated with a capability change more often than persistent spatial ones: persistent mixed events have a median relative capability change of +0.19 (TACO) / +0.16 (ARCTIC) and 46 % of them gain more than 25 % on both datasets (persistent spatial: 20 % / 23 %), amount-dominant events have a median of +0.73 / +0.14, and the onset and release positive controls go from no modelled capability to a grasp and from a grasp to none.
evidence.metric: Same measures as the main entry, by event class of the test split (primary setting): relative change of the direction-averaged support-function capacity Q (0 = unchanged), pre→post retention (1 = PRE grasp already had the POST capability; one-sided), share of events within ±25 % and gaining > 25 %. Medians over events with 95 % take-bootstrap CIs; shares have no CI. Classes: persistent mixed = amount ratio between 0.3 and 0.7, firm contact throughout; amount-dominant = amount ratio ≥ 0.7 (diagnostic); onset / regrasp and release = positive controls; transient = persistence < 0.5 (diagnostic).

caveats: 'More often', not 'always': about half of the persistent mixed events still stay within ±25 % (49 % TACO / 43 % ARCTIC).
The spatial / mixed boundary is a labelled cut of the amount ratio at 0.3; the report says so in its limitations.

The profile cosine barely separates the classes (spatial 0.97 / 0.96 versus mixed 0.95 / 0.95) because a cosine ignores an overall scale change; the separation shows in the relative change, the retention and the shares.

The onset 'relative change' values in the CSV and in the report's Table 1 (about 1e9) are a division by epsilon (Q_pre = 0) and must not be quoted; state the control as 'from 0 to a median Q of 1.20 / 0.78'. Release has retention pre→post = 1 by definition of the one-sided measure, which must not be read as 'release preserves capability'.

The positive controls are close to by-construction (no contact patch at the PRE frame of 69 of 77 / 17 of 19 onset events, none at the POST frame of every release): they show that frames and pipeline line up and that the metric is not flat. The graded response of the mixed and amount-dominant classes is the more informative contrast.
ARCTIC amount-dominant interval is very wide ([0.00, 0.95]); the TACO transient class is a random subsample of 150 of 708 events.
Wrench capability is a modelled proxy in normalised units (see the main entry).

evidence.claim: Within the persistent spatial class, a capability change above 25 % is associated with a change of the set of contacting hand parts (palm and five fingers): events that keep the same set, including those in which parts slide by more than 1 cm, stay within ±25 % in 61 of 62 (TACO) and 15 of 15 (ARCTIC) cases; 23 of the 24 TACO and 6 of the 6 ARCTIC events that gain more than 25 % have a newly touching part, and 8 of 8 / 3 of 3 events that lose more than 25 % have a part leaving (counts over the per-event table, not printed in the report). In the report's own table the median absolute relative change is 0.03 (TACO) / 0.07 (ARCTIC) when no part is reconfigured against 0.18–0.25 with one or more reconfigured parts, where 'reconfigured' counts a part that slid more than 1 cm as well as one that appeared or disappeared; for persistent mixed events the same split gives 0.04 / 0.02 against 0.25–0.73.
evidence.metric: Hand parts = palm + five fingers (MANO skinning-weight labels). A part is 'stable' if it touches before and after with its patch centroid moving ≤ 1 cm, 'slid' if it moved more, 'appeared' / 'disappeared' if it touches only after / only before. The report's Table 5 groups events by the number of reconfigured parts (slid + appeared + disappeared = 0, 1, ≥ 2) and gives the median pre→post retention (1 = preserved) and the median |relative change| of Q (0 = unchanged); no intervals are given. The finger-set split (same set / part added / part removed only) is a count over events.csv rows made in this evidence pass.

'Finger removal' evidence is weaker than 'finger addition': the report discusses additions only; the removal statement rests on the events.csv count (12 TACO / 4 ARCTIC 'removed only' events).

On ARCTIC the retention by number of reconfigured parts is flat for the spatial class (0.90 / 0.91 / 0.88 with only 5 / 6 / 15 events); the gradient is visible in |relative change| and in the mixed class.
On TACO spatial the median |relative change| is not monotone in the number of parts (0.03 / 0.20 / 0.18).
Events that only lose parts have a high one-sided retention although their capability fell; use the relative change for them.
This is an association in observational data under one wrench model, with no intervals in the source table; 'hand part' includes the palm.

With unit budgets per finger, an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction of the model (the report: 'keeping the per-finger limits makes finger additions count'); under a single whole-hand budget the classes move closer (see the sensitivity entry).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: Within the persistent spatial and the persistent mixed class, the size of the capability change is associated with hand parts being added or removed rather than sliding in place: with no reconfigured part the median absolute relative change is 0.03 (TACO) / 0.07 (ARCTIC) for spatial events against 0.18–0.25 with one or more reconfigured parts, and 23 of the 24 TACO and 6 of the 6 ARCTIC persistent spatial events that gain more than 25 % have a hand part newly touching the object.
evidence.correction_reason: Every number is right, but the sentence attaches 'added or removed rather than sliding in place' to the Table-5 split, and that split counts a slid part as reconfigured, so 0.03 / 0.07 versus 0.18-0.25 contrasts 'nothing moved more than 1 cm' with 'something slid, appeared or disappeared' and cannot separate sliding from adding. The sliding-versus-adding contrast is carried by the finger-set counts from events.csv (same set 61 of 62 / 15 of 15 within ±25 %; my recount: slide-only events 32 of 33 TACO and 10 of 10 ARCTIC within ±25 %). 'Removed' rests only on counts made from events.csv (the report discusses additions). The claim also names the mixed class but quoted no mixed number. Association only: with one unit budget per finger an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction.

evidence.claim: The size of the dense contact-map change is only weakly associated with the capability change for persistent spatial events on TACO (Spearman 0.19 with the relative change, −0.27 with the retention, n = 119) and moderately on ARCTIC (0.55 / −0.60, n = 26; no interval is given for these correlations). On TACO this is consistent with the size of the contact change providing little information about the capability change: 33 of the 73 events with a contact change at or above the train median keep |relative change| at or below the train median of 0.13 (45 % [34, 57]). On ARCTIC only 1 of the 11 such events does (9 % [0, 30]; train median 0.09); 5 of the 11 gain more than 25 %.

No interval or p-value is given in the source. Quadrant: among persistent spatial test events whose contact change is at or above the median of the TRAIN persistent spatial events, the share whose |relative change| is at or below the train median; 95 % take-bootstrap CI.

'Small capability change' in the quadrant is a strict cut (|relative change| at or below the train median 0.13 / 0.09), not 'within 25 %'. On ARCTIC, of the 11 large-change events only 5 gain more than 25 % (events.csv); the others change by 0.10–0.25 in magnitude and one is a loss.

Do not quote the report's final-answer sentence '... most of the large-contact-change spatial events (10 of 11), on TACO fewer than half (55 %)': 55 % (40 of 73) is more than half, and the ten ARCTIC events are not all finger-adding gains above 25 %.
The correlation is not zero even for the spatial class on TACO, and it is 0.40 / 0.52 for the mixed class: do not write 'contact-change size is unrelated to capability change'.
evidence.claim_as_extracted: The size of the dense contact-map change is only weakly associated with the capability change for persistent spatial events on TACO (Spearman 0.19 with the relative change, −0.27 with the retention, n = 119) and moderately on ARCTIC (0.55 / −0.60, n = 26), which is consistent with a large dense contact change providing little information about a capability change on TACO, while on ARCTIC the large-change spatial events mostly do change the capability.
evidence.correction_reason: Correlations and quadrant values are exact. 'Mostly do change the capability' is true only against the strict train-median cut (10 of 11 exceed |0.09|); against the ±25 % band used everywhere else on the page it is 5 of 11, so the criterion has to be stated. The ARCTIC statement rests on 11 events and the Spearman values have no interval or p-value in the source.

evidence.claim: The persistent spatial result is stable across ten modelling settings (the primary one and nine one-at-a-time changes of friction, patch merging, contact threshold and force-budget scheme): the median pre→post retention stays between 0.82 and 0.92 on TACO and between 0.76 and 0.94 on ARCTIC, and the median relative change between 0.00 and +0.04 (TACO) and −0.01 and +0.04 (ARCTIC). The largest shifts are the 0.5 cm contact threshold on ARCTIC (retention 0.76 [0.71, 0.81] against 0.89) and the single whole-hand budget, which raises retention to 0.92 (TACO) and 0.94 (ARCTIC). All settings stay inside the same contact-patch model.

caveats: The sensitivity tables are computed over 123 TACO persistent spatial events (the 4 not firm throughout are included) and over 452 / 131 persistent mixed events although the report labels the mixed rows 'firm throughout'; their 'primary' row therefore differs slightly from Table 1 (TACO spatial relative change 0.0322 [0.0011, 0.0585] versus 0.0362 [0.0037, 0.0761]). Retention medians agree.
One setting is varied at a time and all settings stay inside the same model family; this is not robustness to real physics (no mass, inertia or force limits).
The ARCTIC dip at the 0.5 cm threshold (0.76 [0.71, 0.81]) must stay visible; the report explains it by grasps losing contacts on one side, which is an explanation, not a tested result.

The report's statement that the mixed class 'stays clearly above the spatial class in every setting' holds for the medians; with a single whole-hand budget the classes move close (TACO mixed 0.0424 versus spatial 0.0149; ARCTIC mixed 0.0542 [0.00, 0.13] versus spatial −0.0105 [−0.06, 0.08]).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: The persistent spatial result is stable across the ten modelling settings that were varied one at a time: the median pre→post retention stays between 0.76 and 0.94 and the median relative change between −0.01 and +0.04 on both datasets, with the 0.5 cm contact threshold on ARCTIC (retention 0.76) as the one setting that moves a number noticeably.
evidence.correction_reason: Ranges verified from the three sensitivity CSVs (TACO 0.8250-0.9219, ARCTIC 0.7640-0.9433; relative change TACO 0.0-0.0402, ARCTIC -0.0105-0.0410). Two wording problems: there are nine variations plus the primary setting, not ten variations; and 'the one setting that moves a number noticeably' is too strong, because the whole-hand budget moves TACO retention to 0.92 [0.90, 0.93], above the primary interval [0.81, 0.88]. Per-dataset ranges should be shown rather than one union range. Caveat: the TACO sensitivity rows use 123 events, 4 of them with no contact patch at either frame (relative change exactly 0, retention undefined).

evidence.claim: Along the direction of the object's velocity change over the 8 frames after the event start (a force direction; no required wrench is computed), the grasp after a persistent spatial event is not systematically more capable than the grasp before it, transported to the same frame (median post / pre capacity ratio 1.06 [0.98, 1.14] on TACO; 0.94 [0.48, 0.98] on ARCTIC, i.e. slightly below 1), whereas persistent mixed events have ratios of 1.13–1.30 over the force, torque and support directions (8- and 16-frame horizons) with intervals above 1 on both datasets.
evidence.metric: Report's 'Metric B': support-function capacity along three observable directions of the object's future motion — change of translational velocity over K = 8 or 16 frames after the event start (a pure force), change of angular velocity (a pure torque), and world-up (support against gravity). Directions only: no required wrench is computed because mass and inertia are unknown. Here the PRE grasp IS transported to the POST frame (patches kept on their mesh vertex ids; ARCTIC's lid follows the articulation). Ratio = post / pre capacity, median over events, 95 % take-bootstrap CI; 1 = no change, above 1 = POST grasp more capable along that direction.
