caveats: Direction-only analysis: it uses normalised directions of the object's kinematics, never a required wrench; ARCTIC's hinge torque is not turned into a direction, and low-motion windows give noisy directions (report section 12).

On ARCTIC the force ratio at K = 8 is below 1 with an interval that excludes 1 ([0.48, 0.98]): the post grasp is slightly less able along that direction. The report's summary phrase 'intervals including 1' is therefore not exact for this cell.
This supports 'not better aligned with the coming motion under the model'; it is not evidence about human intent and not a null-space measurement (no Jacobian null space was computed).
evidence.claim_as_extracted: Along the directions in which the object is about to move, the grasp after a persistent spatial event is not systematically more capable than the grasp before it (post / pre capacity ratio for the force direction over the next 8 frames: 1.06 [0.98, 1.14] on TACO, 0.94 [0.48, 0.98] on ARCTIC), whereas persistent mixed events have ratios of 1.13–1.30 with intervals above 1 on both datasets.
evidence.correction_reason: Values match the table. Two precision points: the direction is that of the change of translational velocity over K frames after the event START (an acceleration direction), not the direction of motion; and the upper end 1.30 comes from the 16-frame horizon on ARCTIC (1.2956 [1.09, 1.57] force, 1.2976 [1.02, 1.62] torque), which the entry's number list does not contain (verified in the CSV). This is the one measure where the pre grasp is transported by mesh vertex id. Direction-only analysis; no intent or null-space reading.

do_not_claim: 'Spatial contact changes do not matter' or 'all spatial reconfigurations are function-preserving': the result is a median over one event class; 20 % (TACO) / 23 % (ARCTIC) of persistent spatial events gain more than 25 % capability and 8 / 3 events lose more than 25 %.
'Null-space motion' or 'the fingers move in the grasp's null space': no Jacobian or grasp-map null space was measured; the report speaks only of redundancy 'under the modelled wrench constraints'.

'Function-preserving' without the qualifier 'modelled wrench capability' / 'under the modelled constraints': there is no mass, centre of mass, inertia, force limit or friction measurement; it is not a physical feasibility result.
Anything about human intent, comfort, fatigue, slip correction or purposelessness: the report explicitly excludes motive inference; wrench capability is a proxy for functional grasp capability.
'The grasp before retains 85–90 % of the capability in every direction' (the report's own loose phrase): retention is a mean over 76 directions of a capped ratio, and it is one-sided.

'The grasps before and after are equivalent because retention is about 0.85–0.89': retention is one-sided (a shrunken grasp scores about 1); report the reverse retention, cosine or relative change alongside.
'Release preserves capability (retention 1.0)' or 'onset changes capability by a factor of 1e9': both are artifacts (one-sided definition; division by epsilon when Q_pre = 0).
'Retention and cosine are computed after transporting the pre grasp by vertex id': transport is used only for the future-motion directions.
'Persistent mixed events always change capability': about half stay within ±25 % (49 % / 43 %).
'On ARCTIC, large spatial contact changes preserve capability': only 1 of 11 large-change events stays below the train-median change.

The report's sentence 'on ARCTIC these functional regrasps are most of the large-contact-change spatial events (10 of 11), on TACO fewer than half (55 %)': 55 % is more than half and the ten ARCTIC events are not all finger-adding gains above 25 %.
The report's '0.5–2.7 fingers appearing' in the events that gain more than 25 %: not reproduced by events.csv (mean 1.46, range 0–4, on TACO; exactly 1 on ARCTIC).

'Contact-change size is unrelated to capability change': Spearman is 0.19 on TACO but 0.55 on ARCTIC for spatial events, and 0.40 / 0.52 for mixed events; no intervals are given for these correlations.

'Finger additions cause the capability gain' as an established causal result: it is an association in observational data, and with one unit budget per finger an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction of the model.

'Finger removals lower capability' as a report finding: the report discusses additions; the removal pattern (8 of 8 and 3 of 3 loss events have a part disappearing) is a count made from events.csv in this pass.
A pooled number such as '145 events' or a retention averaged over TACO and ARCTIC: the datasets are never pooled.
'The result holds on OakInk2' or 'on all three datasets': OakInk2 was excluded.
'Robust to the physics': the ten sensitivity settings stay inside the same contact-patch model; under the strict single-hand measure retention is 0.66 / 0.75.

'A deterministic contact model cannot predict these events' as a result of this study: it is the report's interpretation; this study measured no prediction error. The word 'missed' rests on the hand-contact predictive-information report ('least explained').

'The Figure F examples are typical': they are selected extremes (highest retention, largest gain among events with an above-median contact change); three of the four 'equivalent' examples actually lost capability (−0.10, −0.17, −0.13).

'Contact does not move over time' or 'post-grasp reconfigurations are rare': persistent spatial events are 123 of 1 464 detected TACO test events and 26 of 283 on ARCTIC, alongside 452 / 131 persistent mixed events that more often change capability.
'The post grasp is never better aligned with the coming motion': true for the spatial class under the direction-only analysis, but the mixed class has ratios of 1.13–1.30 with intervals above 1.

'119 events from 177 takes' or 'the test split has 177 / 37 takes': the events come from 73 / 15 takes, and the fixed test split has 186 / 44 takes (177 / 37 are the takes with at least one detected event).
Units such as newtons or newton-metres for the capability: values are normalised (finger budget = 1, torque divided by the object's largest vertex radius).

evidence.claim_as_extracted: The ladder adds one descriptor block at a time: R0 finger participation (6 numbers per frame), R1 + contact amount (12), R2 + per-part contact centroid and mean contact normal (48), R3 + contact spread and patch count (60), R4 = R2 + coarse hand pose (90), R5 = R3 + coarse hand pose (102), CONTACT_FULL = the dense canonical contact map (512), FULL = dense map + 100 hand surface points (812).

R2 is a function of the dense state, and the report says this is 'a statement about the parameterisation, not about the information' (section 4): a 2-layer probe on about 60-80 k training frames does not decode finger-labelled geometry from the 512 canonical points.

The functional target is the wrench report's modelled, normalised capability (unit finger budgets, linearised friction cone with mu = 0.5, one hand) - a proxy for functional grasp capability, not human force, intent or physical feasibility (report section 10).

Learned probes measure what a fixed small model can extract, not information content (report section 10). The probe also receives the object descriptor G; without G R2 reaches 0.17400455474853513 (TACO) / 0.19105257093906403 (ARCTIC) (functional_probe.csv, probe=mlp).

The amount block (R0 -> R1) lowers the wrench error by 6 % on TACO (0.9430775354468436) and not on ARCTIC (1.0048338404036594); participation alone already halves the train-mean error.

evidence.claim: R2 is close to, but not at, the lowest error: its wrench-probe error is 13 % (TACO) and 8 % (ARCTIC) above the best representation, and its composite future-structure error 4 % (TACO) and 2 % (ARCTIC) above the best.
evidence.metric: Gap to the best representation of each axis = error ratio to the lowest-error representation - 1 (0 = the best; lower is better); brackets = 95 % interval of the paired take bootstrap. Functional axis = wrench-probe relative-L1 error sum; temporal axis = composite T1-T4 error averaged over h = 1, 4, 8.
caveats: Report prose and table disagree on the INTERVAL of R2's temporal gap to the best: the decision table and section 5 print 4.0 % [2.7, 5.2] (TACO) and 1.7 % [-1.8, 5.1] (ARCTIC); saturation_summary.csv and the report's own Table 7 give [0.031, 0.050] and [-0.006, 0.039]. The CSV values are the ones quoted here; the point estimates agree.

Report section 8 names R4 (TACO) and R2 (ARCTIC) as the best temporal representation; saturation_summary.csv column best_temporal is R5 on both datasets (R4 is 0.5 % behind on TACO, R2 1.7 % behind on ARCTIC).
On ARCTIC the interval of R2's temporal gap to the best includes 0; on TACO it does not.
Same fixed-probe and fixed-recipe qualifiers as the other F2-A / F2-B entries.

do_not_claim: That R2 is the optimal, minimal or necessary representation: the ladder is one path through the space of descriptors, R2 is not the lowest-error rung on either axis, and the rule against FULL is passed because FULL is worse under the fixed models.

That the dense contact map contains less information than R2, or that dense detail is irrelevant: R2 is computed from the dense state; the report calls the dense inputs' higher error 'a statement about the parameterisation, not about the information'. 'Over-specified' is page wording, not a measured property.

That R2 predicts the future contact well in absolute terms: the R2-input model is worse than persistence at h = 1 on both datasets and at every horizon on ARCTIC; only the ranking of inputs under one fixed recipe is evidence.
That R2 is sufficient for predicting the dense future contact: from an R2 window the future dense contact map is predicted 1.3-2.3 times worse than from FULL.

That R2 preserves human intent, real grasp stability or physical feasibility: the functional target is a modelled, normalised wrench capability (unit finger budgets, mu = 0.5, one hand) - a proxy for functional grasp capability.

That R2 is only a wrench descriptor, or conversely that its temporal role is established independently of the wrench: one of the four composite targets (T4) is the future wrench profile, and on the temporal axis alone R1 already passes the rule against FULL.
That the residual is noise, random, or (biological / robot) null-space motion: it is persistent, the report says 'not structure and not noise', and no Jacobian null space was measured.

That the residual is unpredictable without qualification: on TACO the causal predictor removes 4 / 14 / 20 % of the last-value error, the hand-point residual partly follows the future structure on both datasets, and 'not predictable' means 'not by these models from this context'.

That '11-15 %' or '26-31 %' are confidence intervals or ranges over runs: the two ends are the contact-map block and the hand-point block; the values are 1 - R2 of one frame-wise decoder (an upper bound, decoder trained to the epoch cap, no object descriptor as input).

That the coarse hand pose is useless or 'adds <= 2 %' everywhere: it lowers the TACO composite by 5 % at h = 8, it helps predict the future hand (x 0.64 / x 0.58) and it lowers the strict-profile error in the one-seed sensitivity.
That topology does not matter: it lowers the wrench-probe error by 10 % (TACO) / 7 % (ARCTIC) and is what the rule selects when the wrench must match the best representation closely.

That all spatial changes are functionally irrelevant or that sliding does not change the wrench: sliding events still change the wrench profile by a median 0.10-0.14, and only 24 % (TACO) / 18 % (ARCTIC) of large dense changes fall in the small-R2-change and small-wrench-change quadrant.
A pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any statement about OakInk2, for these blocks.

That this study shows a generator should be built on R2 or that R2 supervision helps generation: it is a diagnostic with small probes and fixed predictors - no generative model and no rollout were run here.

The report's prose interval '4.0 % [2.7, 5.2]' / '1.7 % [-1.8, 5.1]' for R2's temporal gap to the best, or its section-8 statement that the best temporal representation is R4 (TACO) / R2 (ARCTIC): the tables give [3.1, 5.0] / [-0.6, 3.9] and R5 on both.
That 'finger exchanges change the wrench twice as much as sliding' on both datasets: it holds on ARCTIC only.

That the figG example sheets show 'the same structure with a different dense realization': the 'variation' examples are the largest dense change among events whose R2 change is below the train median (not zero), and the ARCTIC one has a large amount change.

'Sufficient' means sufficient for the modelled wrench proxy and for the structured targets T1-T4 under these fixed models; it is the report's operational term, not a proof of sufficiency or optimality.

do_not_claim: That R2 is the optimal, minimal or necessary representation: the ladder is one path through the space of descriptors, R2 is not the lowest-error rung on either axis, and the rule against FULL is passed because FULL is worse under the fixed models.

That the dense contact map contains less information than R2, or that dense detail is irrelevant: R2 is computed from the dense state; the report calls the dense inputs' higher error 'a statement about the parameterisation, not about the information'. 'Over-specified' is page wording, not a measured property.

That R2 predicts the future contact well in absolute terms: the R2-input model is worse than persistence at h = 1 on both datasets and at every horizon on ARCTIC; only the ranking of inputs under one fixed recipe is evidence.
That R2 is sufficient for predicting the dense future contact: from an R2 window the future dense contact map is predicted 1.3-2.3 times worse than from FULL.

That R2 preserves human intent, real grasp stability or physical feasibility: the functional target is a modelled, normalised wrench capability (unit finger budgets, mu = 0.5, one hand) - a proxy for functional grasp capability.

That R2 is only a wrench descriptor, or conversely that its temporal role is established independently of the wrench: one of the four composite targets (T4) is the future wrench profile, and on the temporal axis alone R1 already passes the rule against FULL.
That the residual is noise, random, or (biological / robot) null-space motion: it is persistent, the report says 'not structure and not noise', and no Jacobian null space was measured.

That the residual is unpredictable without qualification: on TACO the causal predictor removes 4 / 14 / 20 % of the last-value error, the hand-point residual partly follows the future structure on both datasets, and 'not predictable' means 'not by these models from this context'.

That '11-15 %' or '26-31 %' are confidence intervals or ranges over runs: the two ends are the contact-map block and the hand-point block; the values are 1 - R2 of one frame-wise decoder (an upper bound, decoder trained to the epoch cap, no object descriptor as input).

That the coarse hand pose is useless or 'adds <= 2 %' everywhere: it lowers the TACO composite by 5 % at h = 8, it helps predict the future hand (x 0.64 / x 0.58) and it lowers the strict-profile error in the one-seed sensitivity.
That topology does not matter: it lowers the wrench-probe error by 10 % (TACO) / 7 % (ARCTIC) and is what the rule selects when the wrench must match the best representation closely.

That all spatial changes are functionally irrelevant or that sliding does not change the wrench: sliding events still change the wrench profile by a median 0.10-0.14, and only 24 % (TACO) / 18 % (ARCTIC) of large dense changes fall in the small-R2-change and small-wrench-change quadrant.
A pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any statement about OakInk2, for these blocks.

That this study shows a generator should be built on R2 or that R2 supervision helps generation: it is a diagnostic with small probes and fixed predictors - no generative model and no rollout were run here.

The report's prose interval '4.0 % [2.7, 5.2]' / '1.7 % [-1.8, 5.1]' for R2's temporal gap to the best, or its section-8 statement that the best temporal representation is R4 (TACO) / R2 (ARCTIC): the tables give [3.1, 5.0] / [-0.6, 3.9] and R5 on both.
That 'finger exchanges change the wrench twice as much as sliding' on both datasets: it holds on ARCTIC only.

That the figG example sheets show 'the same structure with a different dense realization': the 'variation' examples are the largest dense change among events whose R2 change is below the train median (not zero), and the ARCTIC one has a large amount change.

evidence.claim: With the true initial contact s_0 given, adding the explicit R2 output loss to the deterministic dense generator (D1 versus D0) did not improve it. TACO: participation, centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 1.8-5.4 % higher and the dense error 1.4 % higher (all intervals exclude zero). ARCTIC: centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 3.1-4.9 % higher (intervals exclude zero), while participation (+0.8 % [-2.1, +3.4]) and dense error (+0.7 % [-0.7, +2.0]) are not distinguishable from no change. Of the six reported errors only the contact amount is lower, by under 1 % (TACO -0.9 % [-1.4, -0.4]; ARCTIC -0.8 % [-1.8, +0.3], interval includes zero). This holds for the one surrogate tested (differentiable grid R2 operator, weights 0.3 / 1 / 3, validation chose 0.3).

evidence.claim_as_extracted: With the true initial contact s_0 given, adding the explicit R2 output loss to the deterministic dense generator (D1 versus D0) did not improve it: on TACO the participation, centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 1.8-5.4 % higher with intervals that exclude zero; on ARCTIC centroid, normal and wrench-profile errors are 3.1-4.9 % higher (intervals exclude zero) while participation is not distinguishable from no change; only the contact-amount error improves, by under 1 %.
evidence.correction_reason: All numbers and directions are confirmed in paired_comparisons.csv. Two small imprecisions: 'only the amount improves' is stated without saying that on ARCTIC the amount interval includes zero and the sign differs between seeds (it is only in the caveats), and the claim omits the dense error (worse on TACO, tie on ARCTIC). Scope ('this surrogate under this recipe', report section 16) should travel with the claim.

do_not_claim: Structural (R2) supervision cannot help, or R2 is the wrong structure: only one surrogate (a differentiable grid R2 operator with ground-truth part labels), weights 0.3 / 1 / 3 and one training recipe were tested; nothing between 0 and 0.3. The report's wording is 'this surrogate under this recipe does not help'.

R2 supervision significantly hurts every metric on both datasets: on ARCTIC participation, dense error and amount are not distinguishable from no change, and the amount error improves slightly on TACO.
The output loss gave a 'marginal gain' on TACO (the decision table's 'marginal (< 5 %)' is a rule label; the significant changes are all for the worse except the amount, -0.9 %).
The hidden head makes D2 significantly worse than D0: no paired D2-versus-D0 comparison exists; the claim rests on D2 vs D1 plus D1 vs D0.
Diffusion is worse on structure: at the dense-only level it ties (intervals include zero), and at the hidden-head level one S2 sample is better than D2 on participation / centroid / normal.
'S models are 15-26 % worse on dense error': true for S0 and S1 against their matched deterministic model (14.8-26.6 %), not for S2 vs D2 (+31.8 % TACO, +46.9 % ARCTIC).
'3.7-17x the real frame-to-frame change' as one range: it pools TACO (3.6-6.9x) with ARCTIC (9.8-17.2x) and S0 with S2.

Human futures given s_0 are deterministic or unimodal, or 'universally deterministic': only one future is observed per condition and the tested diffusion recipe is noisy; the supported statement is that this stochastic future model gave no K = 1 structural benefit.

Future stochasticity is unnecessary in general, or 'initial stochasticity is sufficient' as an established fact: 'Case A' is a rule output of aggregate.decision(), which has no branch for a standalone Case C; the report's wording is 'Case A, with a Case-C caveat for this diffusion recipe'.

Best-of-10 gains show that the diffusion captures alternative valid futures: best-of-10 is an oracle against the single observed future, and even then the dense error stays 7.4 % (TACO) / 16.6 % (ARCTIC) worse.

The 2-5x diversity multiplier is a like-for-like decomposition, or 'R2 and wrench diversity are 5x larger': the two sides use different protocols and frame ranges, the multipliers exist only in prose, D_Z and wrench are 2.0-3.2x, and the 5x end is the centroid component.

The initial sampler's diversity is 'meaningful' in the sense of covering real alternative grasps: diversity is a spread, the sampled s_0 are far from the true s_0 (error 2.35 TACO / 2.40 ARCTIC), and no coverage test was run.
The deterministic model reproduces real temporal dynamics: it changes less from frame to frame than the real data (about half on TACO).
D0 is the best model on every metric: it has the lowest dense error on both datasets, but S2 is nominally at or below it on ARCTIC structural metrics.
The generators know which finger touches: structural metrics are extracted with ground-truth hand-part labels; no model outputs finger identity.
This experiment shows that R2 is a useful analysis / relational representation: that comes from the earlier structure / variance study; here R2 was only a training-time loss and an evaluation lens.

The jitter is a sampler or implementation bug, or conversely an inherent property of diffusion: the diagnostic (one seed per dataset, 96 sequences) only shows it does not depend on the number of DDIM steps for this trained model.

End-to-end generation is solved by 'sample s_0, then evolve deterministically': with sampled s_0 the error is dominated by the sampled initial contact, and on ARCTIC the evolved dense error is no lower than holding the sample.
The models were trained to convergence, or the hypotheses were pre-registered: every run stopped by early-stopping patience, and the report does not use the word pre-registered.

Wrench results as statements about human intent, or any robot null-space reading: the wrench profile is a modelled proxy for functional grasp capability (one unit-force friction-cone patch per active hand part).
Any OakInk2 statement for this block, or any number pooled or averaged over TACO and ARCTIC.

evidence.claim: Stage 1 trains, per dataset, a single-frame autoencoder that splits the dense contact map C into a structure-oriented latent z (shaped by its own reconstruction and by a relational loss that matches pairwise z distances to R2 + wrench teacher distances) and a complementary code r that only adds a residual correction on top of the z-only map; the r branch reads z through a stop-gradient and no independence term is used.
evidence.metric: Architecture description (no metric). For the redrawn diagram: C (512 values, one per canonical surface point) and geometry G -> E_z (point transformer over 512 tokens [geo | C], conditioned on G, 4 attention-pool queries) -> z; D_z (geometry tokens only, conditioned on [G | z]) -> z-only map C_bar; E_r (tokens [geo | C | 10 x (C - sg(C_bar))], conditioned on [G | sg(z)]) -> r; D_r (tokens [geo | sg(C_bar)], conditioned on [G | sg(z) | r], output = per-point scalar readout + a structure-conditioned 64-D linear basis combined by r) -> Delta_C; C_hat = C_bar + Delta_C. Losses: L_coarse = MSE(C_bar, C) -> E_z, D_z; L_rel = SmoothL1 between batch-normalised pairwise distances of z and of the teacher (1/2 R2-descriptor distance + 1/2 wrench-profile distance) over the 8128 pairs of a 128-frame batch -> z only; L_full = MSE(C_hat, C) -> E_r, D_r and, through C_bar, the z branch; 0.01 x mean|Delta_C| -> r branch. Phase A trains the z branch alone, phase B adds the r branch (z frozen 3000 steps, 0.1 x lr 3000 steps, then joint).

r is conditional on z by design (E_r and D_r both read z and the z-only map), so the claim under test is role separation, not independence (report Section 3, H4).
Single-frame representation experiment: nothing temporal is trained; trajectories are used only at evaluation time.

The existing fig1_architecture.png carries stale text (zero-init output, lambda_delta 0.05, 0.1 x lr for 2k steps); the final recipe is non-zero FiLM gates, lambda_delta 0.01, 3000 frozen + 3000 slow steps.
The residual branch needed three failed launches before it activated; the reported r is the r of one specific decoder recipe (report Sections 13 and 15).

The primary A2 / A3 phase B started from the z branch of an earlier 16 000-step launch (training logs: 'z branch initialised from A3_seed0_phaseA (16000 steps)'), although report Section 6 also says the runs are from scratch.
Bottleneck variants with a 16-D z (A1_z16, A2_z16, A3_z16) exist and reach the same verdict.

The retention ratio has no interval, and the unpaired 95 % intervals of the underlying probe metrics of z and of the dense map overlap for every quantity that has one on ARCTIC and for all but wrench EV on TACO (probe_metrics.csv lo / hi columns), so 107 % / 110 % should read 'about as well as', not 'more than'. -0.53 is worse than the trivial predictor, which 'little' hides.

evidence.claim: In the proposed model, adding r to z lowers the test reconstruction error of the dense map from 0.449 to 0.151 on TACO and from 0.645 to 0.205 on ARCTIC (mean per-frame L2, lower is better): the L2 error falls by 66 % / 68 %, and the squared error that z alone leaves falls by 73 % / 87 %. r therefore carries complementary dense detail that z does not reconstruct; that detail is a small part of the map (z alone already explains 98.4 % / 95.7 % of its variance).
evidence.metric: E = mean over the unique test frames (TACO 22 938 frames of 186 takes; ARCTIC 11 560 of 44 takes) of the L2 distance between the reconstructed and the true 512-point contact map, in raw contact units (map values in [0, 1]); lower is better. E_zonly uses the z-only map, E_full the z + r map, both of the same model A3. Gain_r = (E_zonly - E_full) / E_zonly (relative reduction of the L2 error). explained_by_r = 1 - sum of squared errors (z + r) / sum of squared errors (z only) (share of the z-residual energy removed). Brackets = 95 % take-cluster bootstrap interval, 1000 resamples (test-set uncertainty, not training variance).

evidence.claim: In latent swaps between structurally similar test frames, the structure of the decoded map follows the frame that supplied z in 97 % (TACO) and 98 % (ARCTIC) of swaps, whereas the transplanted dense detail follows the frame that supplied r in 77 % of swaps on TACO but only 44 % on ARCTIC, which is consistent with a preferential, not a complete, factorization.
evidence.metric: Share of swaps (higher = cleaner role separation). Pairs (A, B) are test frames of the same mesh from different takes whose R2 + wrench teacher distance is in the lowest 20 % of that mesh's cross-take pairs and whose dense distance is above its median; each pair is swapped both ways (decode z of A with r of B and the reverse). 'Structure follows z' = the decoded map's R2 + wrench distance to the z donor is smaller than to the r donor. 'Detail follows r' = the cosine between the added correction and the r donor's own residual is larger than with the host's residual. Brackets = 95 % take-cluster bootstrap interval (1000 resamples, clustered on the z donor's take). Pre-registered thresholds 0.70 (structure) and 0.60 (detail).

'Transfer only partial on ARCTIC' softens a failed threshold: 'partial' is the label of the two-part swap question. do_not_claim: z and r are disentangled / independent. The model has no independence term, E_r and D_r both read z, and the report states the claim is role separation, not disentanglement.

The network discovered the structure / realization boundary by itself. z is taught by a relational R2 + wrench teacher; the same architecture without it (A2) gives a collapsed z with retention 0.77 / 0.63. The block title 'discovers the boundary' overstates this.
z contains more information than the dense map (from 107 % / 110 %). The number is relative to a small probe on the 512-D map, and the probed quantities are the ones the teacher was built from.

r contains no structure, or r is noise. On TACO the r probe recovers part participation well above the trivial predictor; r has an effective rank of about 15 of 64 and removes 73 % / 87 % of the z-residual energy. Call it a realization residual / complementary dense detail.
r is 'anti-structural' on ARCTIC. The negative retention is a probe that is worse than the training mean; the report reads it as overfitting.
r removes 73 % / 87 % of the reconstruction error. That is the squared-error (energy) share; the L2 error falls by 66 % / 68 % (Gain_r).

The swap test shows the model learned that structure lives in z. Structure following z is largely by construction (z-only map plus a small correction that moves the map by 14 % / 16 % of the pair distance); the same 92-96 % appears without the relational loss.
r's detail transfers between frames. It does on TACO (77 %) but not on ARCTIC (44 %); never state the transfer without the dataset.
Articulation causes the ARCTIC transfer failure. The report offers this as a reading; no experiment isolates it.
r is a persistent or sequence-level identity, or a fixed code per grasp. The persistence question is answered 'partial' on both datasets and r tracks the dense residual frame by frame.

r's future is barely predictable beyond the current structure (gain 0.07 / 0.14), or 'from both 0.38 / 0.48'. The gain rests on a joint ridge fit that scores below the fit from r alone in the same table, and 0.38 / 0.48 is not in any table.
r is unpredictable. Its copy-forward R2 eight frames ahead is 0.36 (TACO) / 0.63 (ARCTIC) and only a linear ridge was tried.
The factorization is 4 x better than a standard autoencoder, without saying that A0 is a weak control with a collapsed latent and that linear PCA-128 is the stricter reference (2.3 x / 3.7 x).
r is a large part of the contact map. z alone already explains 98.4 % / 95.7 % of the map variance.
The result is robust to training randomness. One seed per model; every interval is test-set bootstrap uncertainty.
Stage 1 fully justified Stage 2, or Case A. The table answer is 'partial (Case B)'.
The models were trained to convergence or from scratch. Most runs had their best validation step at the last evaluation, and the primary A2 / A3 phase B started from an earlier 16 000-step z branch.
The finding holds on OakInk2 or across datasets in general. Only TACO and ARCTIC were run, separately.

z captures human intent, or the wrench term makes z functional by itself. The wrench profile is a proxy for functional grasp capability, mixed half and half with R2 in the teacher; its separate contribution was not tested.
z-space neighbourhoods are clearly more structural than dense-map neighbourhoods. The margin is small and the unpaired intervals overlap on both datasets.

evidence.claim_as_extracted: Predicting the 63 future contact maps through the Stage-1 structure-oriented latent z (B1) instead of directly (B0) leaves the dense error statistically tied on TACO (paired interval includes zero) and makes it 14.1 % worse on ARCTIC (paired interval excludes zero).
evidence.correction_reason: Values, direction and dataset scope are right. 'makes it worse' reads as a causal statement about the representation, while the report itself lists confounds of the B1-vs-B0 comparison (decoder reads per-point geometry B0 never sees; absolute versus residual output; 4-frame subsampling of the dense loss; checkpoints selected at 4 k versus 79 k / 33 k steps). do_not_claim: 'z failed as a temporal state' or 'z is a bad state' -- the report states the opposite reading: the latent trajectory, if it could be predicted, would be more than enough; what is not supported is that z is an easier prediction target under this formulation.

'Z-mediated generation is better on TACO' without qualification -- the dense error is tied (nominally 1.8 % worse); only four structural / wrench metrics are better, by 2.7-7.0 %, and only at long horizon. 'Case B' is the rule's label, not a dense-error win.
'The structural benefit holds over the whole sequence' -- in the first 16 frames the direct model is better on dense error, participation, centroid, normal and wrench.
'B0 is 42 % better at t = 1-8' -- the report's figure is 'B1 is 42 % worse' (1.146 vs 0.806).
'On ARCTIC z-mediation is worse on every structural metric' -- only the contact amount is worse by the rule; participation, centroid, normal and wrench are within their intervals.
Any pooled or averaged statement across TACO and ARCTIC (for example an average percentage change of B1 versus B0).

'Decoding the teacher z shows what a z-based generator can reach' -- the teacher latent is computed from the true future frames and is unavailable at inference; it bounds what the representation and decoder allow.
'The teacher-z error is three times lower than any model' as a statement for both datasets -- against B0 it is less than a factor of three on ARCTIC (0.709 vs 1.890).
'90 % of the error is caused by latent prediction' as a variance decomposition or causal attribution -- the number is one minus a ratio of squared mean errors.

'The missing copy of s_0 is the cause of the gap' or 'giving the model the encoded s_0 fixes it' -- the report names this asymmetry as a limitation and did not test such a model; the stateful-z / s_0-preserving design is a motivated current hypothesis, not a result.
'z is disentangled from r' or 'z and r are independent' -- nothing here measures that; use 'structure-oriented' / 'structure information is concentrated in z'.

'r is noise' or 'r is useless' -- the result is that a PREDICTED r (not supervised against the Stage-1 r, at checkpoints selected at 4 000 steps) provides little additional information; r remains a realization residual / complementary dense detail.
'Adding r does not damage z' as a positive finding -- the report calls this test vacuous because the r pathway does almost nothing.
'z mediation makes trajectories more stable' or 'closer to the true temporal statistics' -- the deviation from the ground truth's frame-to-frame change is larger for B1 on both datasets.

'The results are robust across seeds' or 'all models were trained to convergence under equal budgets' -- one seed; three latent runs were stopped by hand before the 20 000-step minimum after a preliminary test pass; B0 was selected at 79 k / 33 k steps and the latent models at 4 k.
'The checkpoints were selected with test data' -- they were not (validation only; sanity check 13 passes); what was not test-blind is the decision to stop three runs.
'The comparison isolates the representation' -- B1 / B2 also differ from B0 in decoder geometry access, in absolute versus residual output, and in the frame subsampling of their dense loss.
'B1 beats (or does not beat) persistence on ARCTIC' as a tested statement -- no paired test against persistence exists in the tables (2.157 vs 2.242 are unpaired means).
'The larger direct model B0 is better than the previous D0 on everything' -- on TACO it is worse than the previous D0 on participation and centroid.

'The latent is harder to predict because of poor temporal geometry / because the future is stochastic' -- this report gives no test of the reason; it only reports that about half (TACO) / a third (ARCTIC) of the teacher's variance is predicted.

Any statement about human intent, robot null-space motion, 'contact does not move over time', or universal determinism from these blocks; the wrench profile is a proxy for functional grasp capability only.
Any OakInk2 claim: the experiment has no OakInk2 result.

caveats: This is a design asymmetry the report states as a limitation: B0 predicts a residual around s_0, whereas B1 / B2 decode absolute maps and the Stage-1 encoder is not part of inference, so the latent models have no path that copies the initial map. A large part of the short-horizon gap is this asymmetry.

The experiment does not say what a latent model that is given the encoded s_0 would do; that such a model would close the gap is a motivated current hypothesis (the stateful-z / s_0-preserving experiment), not a result of this report.
Per-frame values are test means without intervals.

The report's dataset explanation (TACO amortises the initial cost because contact changes a lot within the window; ARCTIC never recovers it) is an interpretation consistent with the persistence errors, not a tested mechanism.
One seed; hand-stopped latent runs (report Section 8).

do_not_claim: 'z failed as a temporal state' or 'z is a bad state' -- the report states the opposite reading: the latent trajectory, if it could be predicted, would be more than enough; what is not supported is that z is an easier prediction target under this formulation.

'Z-mediated generation is better on TACO' without qualification -- the dense error is tied (nominally 1.8 % worse); only four structural / wrench metrics are better, by 2.7-7.0 %, and only at long horizon. 'Case B' is the rule's label, not a dense-error win.
'The structural benefit holds over the whole sequence' -- in the first 16 frames the direct model is better on dense error, participation, centroid, normal and wrench.
'B0 is 42 % better at t = 1-8' -- the report's figure is 'B1 is 42 % worse' (1.146 vs 0.806).
'On ARCTIC z-mediation is worse on every structural metric' -- only the contact amount is worse by the rule; participation, centroid, normal and wrench are within their intervals.
Any pooled or averaged statement across TACO and ARCTIC (for example an average percentage change of B1 versus B0).

'Decoding the teacher z shows what a z-based generator can reach' -- the teacher latent is computed from the true future frames and is unavailable at inference; it bounds what the representation and decoder allow.
'The teacher-z error is three times lower than any model' as a statement for both datasets -- against B0 it is less than a factor of three on ARCTIC (0.709 vs 1.890).
'90 % of the error is caused by latent prediction' as a variance decomposition or causal attribution -- the number is one minus a ratio of squared mean errors.

'The missing copy of s_0 is the cause of the gap' or 'giving the model the encoded s_0 fixes it' -- the report names this asymmetry as a limitation and did not test such a model; the stateful-z / s_0-preserving design is a motivated current hypothesis, not a result.
'z is disentangled from r' or 'z and r are independent' -- nothing here measures that; use 'structure-oriented' / 'structure information is concentrated in z'.

'r is noise' or 'r is useless' -- the result is that a PREDICTED r (not supervised against the Stage-1 r, at checkpoints selected at 4 000 steps) provides little additional information; r remains a realization residual / complementary dense detail.
'Adding r does not damage z' as a positive finding -- the report calls this test vacuous because the r pathway does almost nothing.
'z mediation makes trajectories more stable' or 'closer to the true temporal statistics' -- the deviation from the ground truth's frame-to-frame change is larger for B1 on both datasets.

'The results are robust across seeds' or 'all models were trained to convergence under equal budgets' -- one seed; three latent runs were stopped by hand before the 20 000-step minimum after a preliminary test pass; B0 was selected at 79 k / 33 k steps and the latent models at 4 k.
'The checkpoints were selected with test data' -- they were not (validation only; sanity check 13 passes); what was not test-blind is the decision to stop three runs.
'The comparison isolates the representation' -- B1 / B2 also differ from B0 in decoder geometry access, in absolute versus residual output, and in the frame subsampling of their dense loss.
'B1 beats (or does not beat) persistence on ARCTIC' as a tested statement -- no paired test against persistence exists in the tables (2.157 vs 2.242 are unpaired means).
'The larger direct model B0 is better than the previous D0 on everything' -- on TACO it is worse than the previous D0 on participation and centroid.

'The latent is harder to predict because of poor temporal geometry / because the future is stochastic' -- this report gives no test of the reason; it only reports that about half (TACO) / a third (ARCTIC) of the teacher's variance is predicted.

Any statement about human intent, robot null-space motion, 'contact does not move over time', or universal determinism from these blocks; the wrench profile is a proxy for functional grasp capability only.
Any OakInk2 claim: the experiment has no OakInk2 result.

The comparison of Δz with ΔC in size relies on the random-pair normalisation of each quantity; it is the report's own comparison.
Report Section 12: a temporal-smoothness term for z is 'neither indicated nor ruled out by this study'.

do_not_claim: Do not write that z's temporal behaviour is 'not the problem' or that the representation is cleared as a cause of the Stage-2 failure: only 'Case C as pre-registered (the steps of z do not follow the steps of the contact)' is rejected, and whether z's lower persistence than the dense map contributed was not tested.

Do not write 'the learned predictor beats persistence' for ARCTIC, or without the window-average qualifier: ARCTIC is -2.6 % / 0.2 % / 6.9 % (no / no / marginal), with intervals including zero at h = 1 and 4.

Do not write that ARCTIC z 'has no dynamics', 'is static' or that 'nothing beyond persistence is learnable': at the first frame of a window the ARCTIC gain is 23-28 %, and the ridge reference beats persistence at all three horizons.
Do not write 'the gain is smaller for later pairs on both datasets': on ARCTIC the probe is significantly worse than persistence at h = 1 for pairs starting at t >= 8 and indistinguishable at h = 4.

Do not present the window-position split (or the subject split, the linear references, the trajectory contrast, the composition of the exceptions) as pre-registered results or as rule inputs: they are post hoc ('interpretation, not verdicts').

Do not read the case letters as causes: 'Case A = Stage 2 failed because of open-loop prediction' and 'Case B = z has no learnable dynamics' are the pre-registered READINGS, which the decision table itself marks as not tested (no rollout, no horizon beyond 8) or as a window-average statement.

Do not write that a mixture of both causes was found, that neither hypothesis explains the Stage-2 failure, or that Q5 is answered: the report says 'not decided between A and B' and 'It is not a finding that both causes contribute'.

Do not write that a stateful / iterative / closed-loop z model will or does work better: no closed-loop rollout and no horizon beyond eight frames were measured; the report says 'its benefit is not established'. The stateful-z experiment is a motivated current hypothesis, not a result.

Do not call the probe result 'the dynamics of z' in an autonomous or causal sense: the probe is given the TRUE current latent plus the object-trajectory windows of frames t and t+h (including future object states), it is a single-step teacher-forced prediction, and on TACO about 60 % of its gain is linear in z_t alone.
Do not equate a latent gain with better contact: through the frozen decoder the gain appears only on TACO at h = 8, and on ARCTIC not at all.
Do not extrapolate the growth of the gain with the horizon (3 / 11 / 18 % on TACO) beyond h = 8.
Do not state the gains as seed-robust or as estimates of what is learnable: one seed, one probe family, early-stopped; the report calls them lower bounds on what is learnable.

Do not call the ARCTIC result a cross-subject artefact: on seen-subject test takes the labels are also no / no / marginal, and for t >= 8 the probe is as far below persistence on seen subjects (-8.2 %) as on the unseen one (-9.0 %).
Do not write that the articulated-geometry input explains the ARCTIC exceptions: the report says 'consistent with' and 'No ablation of the geometry input was run to confirm it'.
Do not pool or average the datasets (no 'Spearman 0.83 overall', no '0.4 % of transitions').

Do not present 0.2 % / 0.6 % as a per-horizon value (it is the mean over h = 1, 4, 8; ARCTIC is 0.7 % at h = 4) or the 7.5 % / 8.5 % independence expectation as a horizon mean (it is the h = 4 value).

Do not call the low-ΔC / high-Δz transitions 'errors' or 'noise' of the encoder: on TACO about a third to a half of them carry a structural (participation / teacher) step, i.e. z responds to the structure it was trained on at a small L2 footprint.
Do not write 'contact does not move over time' or 'z is smooth' without qualification: z moves 1.5-2.2 times as far as the dense map in random-pair units and is less persistent than C.

Do not describe the rule as externally pre-registered: say it was fixed in the code before the probes were trained, according to the report (no independent timestamp; one disclosed edit for the validation interval; the rule implementation was corrected once after review, cases unchanged).
Do not use 'disentangled', 'independent', 'proves', 'causes' or 'necessary' for anything in these blocks; z is 'structure-oriented' in the report's own wording.

Report: 'Nothing here shows that z should be discarded. Nothing here shows either that an iterative z_t -> z_{t+1} model would beat Stage 2 at long horizons: no horizon beyond eight frames and no closed-loop rollout were measured.' A stateful / iterative latent model is 'the candidate the rule points to on TACO (Case A); its benefit is not established'.

'Pre-registered' is the report's own statement (thresholds written into zt_common.DECISION before any probe was trained; the file was edited once afterwards for the validation interval only; the rule implementation was corrected once after review to match the written rule, cases unchanged). There is no external registration or independent timestamp.
One seed per probe; the Stage-2 comparison uses the saved predictions of one Stage-2 B1 model.
evidence.claim_as_extracted: The rule fixed before the probes were trained returns Case A on TACO, which the report calls borderline, and Case B on ARCTIC; the report states that these measurements do not decide whether the Stage-2 difficulty came from the open-loop formulation or from little learnable change of z beyond persistence (Q5: not decided), because neither a closed-loop rollout nor a horizon beyond eight frames was measured.
evidence.correction_reason: Cases and Q5 status confirmed (decision_summary.csv, experiment_config.json, report.md lines 7, 26, 28, 512). The report joins the two facts with 'and' (rule split; no rollout / no horizon > 8) and does not say the non-decision is solely 'because' of the missing rollout; the report also says the split 'is not a finding that both causes contribute'. Add 'according to the report' to the timing of the rule (no independent timestamp; zt_common.py mtime 00:11:16 on 2026-10-04 precedes the retained probe logs 00:13-00:26 and the test evaluation logs 01:08, which is consistent with the report but is only a file timestamp).

do_not_claim: Do not write that z's temporal behaviour is 'not the problem' or that the representation is cleared as a cause of the Stage-2 failure: only 'Case C as pre-registered (the steps of z do not follow the steps of the contact)' is rejected, and whether z's lower persistence than the dense map contributed was not tested.

Do not write 'the learned predictor beats persistence' for ARCTIC, or without the window-average qualifier: ARCTIC is -2.6 % / 0.2 % / 6.9 % (no / no / marginal), with intervals including zero at h = 1 and 4.

Do not write that ARCTIC z 'has no dynamics', 'is static' or that 'nothing beyond persistence is learnable': at the first frame of a window the ARCTIC gain is 23-28 %, and the ridge reference beats persistence at all three horizons.
Do not write 'the gain is smaller for later pairs on both datasets': on ARCTIC the probe is significantly worse than persistence at h = 1 for pairs starting at t >= 8 and indistinguishable at h = 4.

Do not present the window-position split (or the subject split, the linear references, the trajectory contrast, the composition of the exceptions) as pre-registered results or as rule inputs: they are post hoc ('interpretation, not verdicts').

Do not read the case letters as causes: 'Case A = Stage 2 failed because of open-loop prediction' and 'Case B = z has no learnable dynamics' are the pre-registered READINGS, which the decision table itself marks as not tested (no rollout, no horizon beyond 8) or as a window-average statement.

Do not write that a mixture of both causes was found, that neither hypothesis explains the Stage-2 failure, or that Q5 is answered: the report says 'not decided between A and B' and 'It is not a finding that both causes contribute'.

Do not write that a stateful / iterative / closed-loop z model will or does work better: no closed-loop rollout and no horizon beyond eight frames were measured; the report says 'its benefit is not established'. The stateful-z experiment is a motivated current hypothesis, not a result.

Do not call the probe result 'the dynamics of z' in an autonomous or causal sense: the probe is given the TRUE current latent plus the object-trajectory windows of frames t and t+h (including future object states), it is a single-step teacher-forced prediction, and on TACO about 60 % of its gain is linear in z_t alone.
Do not equate a latent gain with better contact: through the frozen decoder the gain appears only on TACO at h = 8, and on ARCTIC not at all.
Do not extrapolate the growth of the gain with the horizon (3 / 11 / 18 % on TACO) beyond h = 8.
Do not state the gains as seed-robust or as estimates of what is learnable: one seed, one probe family, early-stopped; the report calls them lower bounds on what is learnable.

Do not call the ARCTIC result a cross-subject artefact: on seen-subject test takes the labels are also no / no / marginal, and for t >= 8 the probe is as far below persistence on seen subjects (-8.2 %) as on the unseen one (-9.0 %).
Do not write that the articulated-geometry input explains the ARCTIC exceptions: the report says 'consistent with' and 'No ablation of the geometry input was run to confirm it'.
Do not pool or average the datasets (no 'Spearman 0.83 overall', no '0.4 % of transitions').

Do not present 0.2 % / 0.6 % as a per-horizon value (it is the mean over h = 1, 4, 8; ARCTIC is 0.7 % at h = 4) or the 7.5 % / 8.5 % independence expectation as a horizon mean (it is the h = 4 value).

Do not call the low-ΔC / high-Δz transitions 'errors' or 'noise' of the encoder: on TACO about a third to a half of them carry a structural (participation / teacher) step, i.e. z responds to the structure it was trained on at a small L2 footprint.
Do not write 'contact does not move over time' or 'z is smooth' without qualification: z moves 1.5-2.2 times as far as the dense map in random-pair units and is less persistent than C.

Do not describe the rule as externally pre-registered: say it was fixed in the code before the probes were trained, according to the report (no independent timestamp; one disclosed edit for the validation interval; the rule implementation was corrected once after review, cases unchanged).
Do not use 'disentangled', 'independent', 'proves', 'causes' or 'necessary' for anything in these blocks; z is 'structure-oriented' in the report's own wording.

M2 differs from M1 in three things changed together (2 extra decoder blocks at width 256, a longer schedule with no stop before 25 000 steps, selection on validation L_C instead of L_C + L_z), not in 'joint versus frozen'; the three are not separated from each other.

The TACO verdict is a close call: the interval excludes 0 and the size (1.96 %) is just under the 2 % threshold; the report says a second training seed could move it to either side. Every model has one training seed; intervals describe the test takes, not training randomness.

The TACO gain is absent at a matched step (M2's state at step 4000 is +0.46 % against M1, similar); the report states this does not cleanly separate selection from capacity. That the gain 'travels with the predicted z, not the decoder' is the report's reading of the swapped-decoder table (old decoder on M2's latents 1.693 against 1.732 on its own); no paired test of that exact comparison exists in the tables.

'Similar' applies to the dense error. 'Longer budget' needs its qualifier: both M2 runs stopped by the patience rule at 25 000 steps (the earliest allowed) and the selected states are step 7000 (TACO) and 8000 (ARCTIC); M1 ran 20 000 (TACO) and 18 000 (ARCTIC, stopped by hand) and was selected at step 4000.

Untested: a wider decoder (the plan recommended 512-768), the 4-block control under the M2 protocol, and a decoder trained on many held-out predictions. The source conclusion is 'no evidence that decoder mismatch caused the failure', not 'decoder mismatch is excluded'.

No evidence was found that this mismatch caused the failure': only two extra blocks at width 256, a longer budget, selection on the dense loss and two small held-out probes were tested; a wider decoder and a decoder trained on many held-out predictions were not.
'A jointly trained decoder was compared with a frozen decoder.' M1 was already trained end to end on the predicted z; M2 differs in capacity, budget and selection, changed together.

'M2 equals M1' or 'no difference at all'. The verdict 'similar' is for the dense error under the 2 % + interval rule; on TACO the interval excludes 0, and participation and frames 1-8 are 'better' on both datasets while the ARCTIC frame-to-frame deviation is 'worse'.

'The TACO improvement is not significant' or, conversely, 'M2 improves on M1 on TACO'. It is resolved (interval excludes 0) and below the size threshold fixed in advance; one seed, 'a second seed could move it to either side'.
'The TACO gain comes from the larger decoder.' It is absent at a matched step and the report reads it as travelling with the predicted latent; selection, capacity and budget are not separated.
'The old and the new decoder produce the same maps.' They reach the same dense error on the same predicted latent.
'The decoder never saw test-sized latent errors during training.' It did in roughly its first thousand steps.
'M2 was trained much longer (100 k steps).' Both M2 runs stopped by the patience rule at 25 000 steps and were selected at step 7000 / 8000.

'The remaining bottleneck is proven to be z trajectory prediction.' The source says 'Most likely yes' and that the latent error cannot be separated from the decoder's sensitivity to it; a second, smaller part is the first frames, where the latent path cannot continue s_0.
'Random latent noise explains 78-90 % of the teacher-to-predicted gap.' Those shares are of the predicted-latent dense error, not of the gap.
'The temporal network memorises the training set and that causes the failure' as an established cause, or any claim about regularisation, data size or model size fixing it: no such ablation was run.

'Held-out adaptation of the decoder does not help' as a general statement. Two small probes on 141 / 106 validation sequences found no gain; Probe A chose zero steps (likely overfitting, fitting-fold error not recorded) and 'cannot bound what a decoder trained on many held-out predictions could do'.
'The teacher z error 0.51 / 0.69 is what a better z predictor would achieve at generation time.' The teacher z* is computed from the true future frames; it is a decoder floor.

'z-mediated generation is better for structure' without the qualifiers: TACO only, already true for M1 before the decoder changes, arising only from frame 17 on, with frames 1-8 worse than the direct model; on ARCTIC there is no structural advantage and the amount is worse.
'z-mediated models beat the persistence baseline on ARCTIC.' No paired test exists; 2.158 vs 2.242 with overlapping intervals, and persistence is lower in frames 1-8.
'ARCTIC is exactly 14 % worse than direct prediction' as a property of the method: the reused direct model may understate direct prediction on ARCTIC (budget-parity run stopped unfinished).
'The Stage-1 z is a poor representation' or 'z is at fault'. The source: 'The Stage-1 z is not shown to be at fault'.
'Decoder adaptation cannot beat the direct model' as a fact. It is an ideal-predictor argument in the report ('an argument, not a measurement').

'This result shows that a stateful / recurrent z model will fix the problem' or presenting the stateful-z experiment as a result: the report says 'Proposed, not shown'; it is a motivated current hypothesis.
Any pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any OakInk2 statement for these blocks.
'Wrench error measures human intent'; wrench relative L1 is a proxy for functional grasp capability.
Reading the overlapping unpaired intervals of the per-model bars as the test: the verdicts come from paired differences on identical sequences.
Results for the optional models M3 (decoder also fed the teacher latent) and M0r (direct model retrained): both were stopped unfinished and have validation-log numbers only, no test evaluation.

do_not_claim: 'Decoder mismatch is not the bottleneck' / 'the decoder is excluded as the cause'. The source says 'Not shown ... No evidence was found that this mismatch caused the failure': only two extra blocks at width 256, a longer budget, selection on the dense loss and two small held-out probes were tested; a wider decoder and a decoder trained on many held-out predictions were not.
'A jointly trained decoder was compared with a frozen decoder.' M1 was already trained end to end on the predicted z; M2 differs in capacity, budget and selection, changed together.

'M2 equals M1' or 'no difference at all'. The verdict 'similar' is for the dense error under the 2 % + interval rule; on TACO the interval excludes 0, and participation and frames 1-8 are 'better' on both datasets while the ARCTIC frame-to-frame deviation is 'worse'.

'The TACO improvement is not significant' or, conversely, 'M2 improves on M1 on TACO'. It is resolved (interval excludes 0) and below the size threshold fixed in advance; one seed, 'a second seed could move it to either side'.
'The TACO gain comes from the larger decoder.' It is absent at a matched step and the report reads it as travelling with the predicted latent; selection, capacity and budget are not separated.
'The old and the new decoder produce the same maps.' They reach the same dense error on the same predicted latent.
'The decoder never saw test-sized latent errors during training.' It did in roughly its first thousand steps.
'M2 was trained much longer (100 k steps).' Both M2 runs stopped by the patience rule at 25 000 steps and were selected at step 7000 / 8000.

'The remaining bottleneck is proven to be z trajectory prediction.' The source says 'Most likely yes' and that the latent error cannot be separated from the decoder's sensitivity to it; a second, smaller part is the first frames, where the latent path cannot continue s_0.
'Random latent noise explains 78-90 % of the teacher-to-predicted gap.' Those shares are of the predicted-latent dense error, not of the gap.
'The temporal network memorises the training set and that causes the failure' as an established cause, or any claim about regularisation, data size or model size fixing it: no such ablation was run.

'Held-out adaptation of the decoder does not help' as a general statement. Two small probes on 141 / 106 validation sequences found no gain; Probe A chose zero steps (likely overfitting, fitting-fold error not recorded) and 'cannot bound what a decoder trained on many held-out predictions could do'.
'The teacher z error 0.51 / 0.69 is what a better z predictor would achieve at generation time.' The teacher z* is computed from the true future frames; it is a decoder floor.

'z-mediated generation is better for structure' without the qualifiers: TACO only, already true for M1 before the decoder changes, arising only from frame 17 on, with frames 1-8 worse than the direct model; on ARCTIC there is no structural advantage and the amount is worse.
'z-mediated models beat the persistence baseline on ARCTIC.' No paired test exists; 2.158 vs 2.242 with overlapping intervals, and persistence is lower in frames 1-8.
'ARCTIC is exactly 14 % worse than direct prediction' as a property of the method: the reused direct model may understate direct prediction on ARCTIC (budget-parity run stopped unfinished).
'The Stage-1 z is a poor representation' or 'z is at fault'. The source: 'The Stage-1 z is not shown to be at fault'.
'Decoder adaptation cannot beat the direct model' as a fact. It is an ideal-predictor argument in the report ('an argument, not a measurement').

'This result shows that a stateful / recurrent z model will fix the problem' or presenting the stateful-z experiment as a result: the report says 'Proposed, not shown'; it is a motivated current hypothesis.
Any pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC number, or any OakInk2 statement for these blocks.
'Wrench error measures human intent'; wrench relative L1 is a proxy for functional grasp capability.
Reading the overlapping unpaired intervals of the per-model bars as the test: the verdicts come from paired differences on identical sequences.
Results for the optional models M3 (decoder also fed the teacher latent) and M0r (direct model retrained): both were stopped unfinished and have validation-log numbers only, no test evaluation.

evidence.claim: The two hypotheses are motivated by earlier finished studies, read per dataset. After the decoder was adapted, the z-mediated model was similar to the direct model in dense error on TACO (E_C 1.698 vs 1.700, verdict similar, with better structure / wrench) and worse on ARCTIC (2.158 vs 1.890, 14.2 % worse). On both datasets its latent error is small on training sequences and large on test sequences (z RMSE 0.088 vs 0.702 on TACO, 0.064 vs 0.717 on ARCTIC), and it is worse than the direct model in frames 1-8 (dense-error gap 0.294 on TACO, 0.481 on ARCTIC). Given the true current z, a learned predictor improves on persistence on TACO at 4 and 8 frames ahead (11.3 % [10.0, 12.5] and 17.8 % [16.5, 19.1] lower RMSE); on ARCTIC the gain is not distinguishable from zero at 4 frames (0.2 % [-4.0, 4.0]) and small at 8 frames (6.9 % [1.6, 12.2]). These are window-averaged direct predictions from the true latent, not rollouts; the predecessor report states that the diagnostic 'did not show that an iterative model would beat Stage 2' and rates the stateful test 'a reasonable next test on TACO and a weak one on ARCTIC'.

evidence.claim: The experiment's code contains a decision rule written down in advance. A paired difference on identical test sequences counts as better or worse only if it is at least 2 % and its 95 % take-cluster bootstrap interval excludes zero; this threshold is the rule of the previous studies and the template describes it as fixed before any result was read. From these verdicts the code assigns each dataset an outcome: A (stateful is the main fix), B (s_0 preservation is the main fix), C (both help: M11 better than M00, M01 and M10), E (nothing beats M00 or D0), or 'mixed' when none applies; D (stateful helps on TACO only) is a separate statement about the two datasets together. The timing cannot be checked independently: the code directory is not under version control and was still being edited while the runs were in progress.
evidence.metric: Rule for reading the planned comparisons; primary metric dense error E_C on test sequences (lower is better); intervals are 95 % paired take-cluster bootstrap intervals (1000 replicates) of the mean per-sequence difference.

evidence.claim: Apart from the two factors, the four z models share the earlier setting: the same data, split, 64-frame sequences, Stage-1 teacher latents, decoder family and size, optimiser, 100 000-step budget with no stop before 25 000 steps, selection on validation L_C, seed and evaluation code, and z only (no r, no diffusion, no new latent). Each factor is a bundle rather than a single change. The stateful level replaces the transformer backbone by an initial-state module plus a residual-MLP transition, adds the loss term L_z0, has fewer parameters (stated design bound: within 15 %), and sees a local window of the object trajectory instead of the whole trajectory. The s_0-preserving level both feeds s_0 to the decoder and decodes a change from s_0. The reused direct reference D0 was trained under the older 80 000-step budget.

do_not_claim: Any result, direction or size of effect of the 2 x 2 experiment (e.g. 'stateful z improves ...', 's_0-preserving decoding fixes early frames', 'M11 is best'): 0 of 6 runs have finished and no test metric of this study exists.

Any preliminary value: validation readings in the training logs or W&B, pilot RMSEs / ratios in init_aug_decision.json, the dry-run metric files in a scratch directory outside the result tree, or numbers from the discarded attempts.
That M00 is a new or retrained run: it is the reused M2 of the z joint-decoder follow-up; only M01, M10 and M11 are trained here. D0 is also reused.
That the previous model 'discards s_0' or 'does not use s_0': only its decoder lacks s_0; the whole-sequence temporal backbone is conditioned on s_0.

That the stateful model is 'closed-loop', 'feedback-controlled', 'teacher-forced' or 'conditioned on observed contact during the rollout': it is a free rollout that feeds back its own predicted latent and depends on (s_0, G, tau) only.

That the stateful model starts from the Stage-1 encoder (z_0 = E_z(s_0)): z_hat_0 comes from a separately trained module with the same architecture; the Stage-1 encoder is not part of the model or of inference.

That the transition is a transformer or a recurrent network with a hidden state, or that z_t+1 depends on z_t alone: it is a residual MLP on the 64-D latent state that also reads G and a 5-frame object-trajectory window (4-frame look-ahead).

That the hypotheses are established causes of the earlier shortfall ('the problem is open-loop prediction', 'the cause is the loss of s_0'): the templates call them remaining, untested architectural assumptions; one planned outcome is 'neither'.

That the experiment is expected to make z-mediated generation beat the direct model: the predecessor report says the diagnostic 'did not show that an iterative model would beat Stage 2' and names as the realistic target 'equal dense error with better structure, without the early-frame loss' (the TACO pattern), and calls the test weak on ARCTIC.

That the decision rule is formally pre-registered or externally time-stamped: it is a dict in a code file that was untracked when this was checked; supported wording is 'fixed in code before any result was read' (the template's claim, not independently verifiable).

'No test quantity was computed before training ended' as a factual statement about the project: a pipeline dry run produced test-part metric files from early snapshots in a scratch directory (selection is nevertheless on validation L_C only).
Pooled or averaged TACO + ARCTIC statements; Case D compares per-dataset answers and is not a pooled number.
That OakInk2 is part of this experiment.
That r, diffusion, new latents or extra losses are involved: the study uses z only, with L_C + L_z (+ L_z0).
That results are multi-seed or cross-validated: one training seed on one fixed split; a second seed is conditional on the ambiguity rule.
That 'z_1:T' frames are predicted with T the window length: 63 future frames (1..63) of a 64-frame window are generated; frame 0 is the given s_0.
That the stateful and whole-sequence models have identical capacity: the stateful models are smaller (design bound in the code: within 15 %).
That the absolute and s_0-preserving decoders differ in size or family: same 6-block width-256 decoder, one extra input column.

That the stateful runs have been running since the first launch: all stateful runs were discarded and restarted from step 1 at 15:44-15:47 on 2026-10-04 after an initialisation defect was found; the discarded runs are used nowhere.
Describing the s_0-preserving change as r, 'noise removal' or a 'null-space' residual: Delta_C_t is the decoded change of the contact map from s_0, nothing more.
Calling z 'disentangled' or 'independent' when describing why it is kept: the sources use a 64-D structure latent from Stage 1; stay with 'structure-oriented'.
